Park scales run environment for both teams.
Temperature and wind modify scoring and so margins.
Zone size modestly shifts walks, strikeouts and runs.
Fielding and framing adjust runs allowed.
Late scratches or IL moves change the lineup or starter after markets open.
Record vs run differential gap measures luck to regress.
Run-difference distribution needed for spread and margin rungs.
Ghost-runner extras settle ties in including-extras contracts.
Price moves after lineup confirmation show how news was priced.
Sharp-line benchmark for fair probability.
Spread and depth decide whether a modelled edge survives execution costs.
Price-dependent fees set the breakeven probability for the edge.
Trade flow around lineup confirmation shows speed and direction of information incorporation.
Settlement values calibrate the model and expose extra-innings, shortened-game and correction edge cases.

interactions.hypothesis: Starter quality only matters for the innings he pitches, so starter edge should be weighted by expected batters faced and the quality gap to the bullpen that replaces him.
Lineup handedness against starter handedness: a platoon-weak confirmed lineup lowers team strength more than season-level wRC+ suggests, so team offence should be lineup-by-hand specific.
Wind and park interact: wind-out adds more runs in HR-friendly parks and for fly-ball pitchers, so the effect should be multiplied with park HR factor and pitcher fly-ball rate.

game_total.target: Total runs (or one team's runs) in the game, with the contract defining whether extra-innings runs count and how shortened games settle.
game_total.mechanism: Expected runs are the sum over plate appearances of per-PA run value, determined by starter quality for the early innings, bullpen quality for the late innings, the lineups' quality by handedness, park and weather (air density, wind), and the umpire's zone. Run distributions are overdispersed and clustered by inning, so threshold prices depend on dispersion and not just the mean; late-breaking information (confirmed lineups, wind, roof status, scratched starters) is the main source of mispricing.

inputs.why: Both starters' run prevention for the early and middle innings.
Innings the starter covers before the bullpen.
Availability determines late-inning scoring.
Quality of relievers beyond workload snapshots.
Lineup offensive quality vs opposing starter handedness.
Confirmed lineup changes offence materially.
Run factors differ widely by park.
Temperature and wind shift scoring.
Wind relative to the field axis rather than compass direction.
Carry of fly balls depends on density.
Zone size shifts walks and runs.
Contact quality and defence determine hits allowed.
Overdispersion and tail shape for rungs.
League baseline run environment for the season.
Extra innings add runs if counted.
Total rungs must imply a coherent distribution.
PA-level simulation propagates lineup, starter, park and weather inputs consistently into total distributions.

interactions.hypothesis: Wind, temperature and park multiply: the same wind adds more in a HR-friendly park and in hot, thin air, so the weather effect must be estimated with park interaction terms.

Starter quality x expected innings x bullpen quality: run total is a mixture of starter-run-rate and bullpen-run-rate by innings, so the starter's hook probability interacts with the bullpen's quality.
Umpire zone x pitcher type: a large zone lowers totals more for hitters' counts and for command pitchers than for high-walk pitchers, so the umpire effect depends on pitcher walk profile.

player_hit.target: Hitter counting outcomes in a game: hits, total bases, RBIs, runs or stolen bases (threshold ladders), requiring the player to appear per the wording.
player_hit.mechanism: Each count is the sum over the hitter's plate appearances of per-PA outcome probabilities, so expected value = expected PA (lineup slot, team scoring, substitution risk) x per-PA rates (contact quality, K/BB, platoon, pitch-type matchup, park, weather, defence) with the opposing starter's quality for the first two or three PAs and the bullpen for the rest. RBI, runs and SB additionally depend on teammates' on-base and the situation, making them more variable and less skill-pure.

inputs.why: PA volume by lineup slot and team total is the multiplier.
Per-PA outcome rates are the base.
Contact quality predicts hits and total bases beyond results.
Handedness matchup with the starter and relievers.
Matchup of hitter's pitch-type weaknesses vs the starter's arsenal.
Starter quality adjusts per-PA outcomes in early PAs.
Bullpen quality for later PAs.
Confirmed batting slot and participation.
Park hit/TB factors by handedness.
Weather influences ball carry and extra-base hits.
Defence converts contact to outs.
BABIP luck regression for hits.
Count distribution given PA and rates.
Runners on base ahead for RBIs.
Steal context for SB legs: steal attempts depend on the runner, the pitcher's delivery time to the plate and the catcher's throw.
Hits/TB rungs for one player are nested.
Head-to-head history is quoted often but is tiny-sample; included to test the null against pitch-type matchup.

interactions.hypothesis: PA count x per-PA probability: a bottom-order hitter with equal skill gets fewer PAs; expected hits thus depend jointly on slot and team total.
Pitch-type matchup x platoon: a hitter's weakness to breaking balls matters more against same-handed breaking-ball-heavy starters, so platoon and pitch-mix effects should be modelled jointly.
BABIP luck x contact quality: recent hit totals overstate skill when xBA lags, so xBA-based projections should replace observed hits.

period.target: First-five-innings (F5) results and totals (and similar inning-window markets): winner, margin and total runs through a set inning.
period.mechanism: F5 isolates starters: run scoring is determined by the starters' quality over their first two trips through the order, the lineups' strength against them, park and weather, with the bullpen entering only when the starter is pulled early. Starter exit probability before the fifth is the major structural uncertainty and ties are possible, so rules matter (push vs loss).

inputs.why: Starter talent dominates the first five innings.
Separates the starter-only portion from the bullpen.
Third-time-through penalty affects innings 5-6.
Probability of early exit before the fifth.
Lineup vs starter handedness: a team's lineup quality against the starter's handedness determines runs in the early innings, more than overall season team offence.
Confirmed batting order: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Run environment for early innings.
Weather scaling: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Zone effects on early innings.
Contact allowed and defence: hits allowed depend on the quality of contact against a pitcher and the fielders converting it into outs.
Overdispersed distribution for the first five.
Tie/push treatment and shortened-game handling.

interactions.hypothesis: Starter exit before the fifth is a mixture: P(early exit) x bullpen quality vs P(full five) x starter quality, so leash and bullpen state interact with starter quality in F5.
Top-of-order exposure: in F5 each starter faces the top of the order twice or more, so top-of-order quality vs handedness is heavier-weighted than in full game.
F5 tie probability is high enough that spread/winner contracts differ by tie rule; the rules interact with run-distribution shape.

player_pitch.target: Starting pitcher counting stats: strikeouts or outs recorded in the game (threshold ladder), requiring the pitcher to start per the wording.
player_pitch.mechanism: Strikeouts = batters faced x per-PA K probability and outs = batters faced x (1 - on-base events), so the outcome is workload times rate. Workload (batters faced) is limited by the pitch cap divided by pitches per PA and by performance-based hooks (the manager's leash, times-through-order, score), while the per-PA K probability combines the pitcher's pitch-level whiff ability with the confirmed lineup's whiff and K tendencies by handedness, modulated by the umpire's zone, catcher framing and park, and diminishing across the order. Realized pitch count is not known pregame; only its distribution is.

inputs.why: Pitcher K%/CSW and opposing-lineup K% by handedness.
Pitch-level whiff drives strikeouts.
Confirmed lineup vulnerability to the pitcher's arsenal.
Platoon-adjusted lineup K% for the confirmed order.
Expected batters faced is the volume multiplier.
Manager hook patterns and pitch cap.
Rehab/return caps truncate the outing.
Pitches per PA scale batters faced under a cap.
Lineup patience reduces BF per pitch.
Times-through-order penalty lowers K late and affects pull.
Zone size alters called strikes.
Extra strikes from receiving: a catcher who gets more borderline pitches called strikes raises the pitcher's strikeout and lowers walk rates.
Velocity changes indicate fatigue or injury.
Bullpen availability influences the hook.
Park/altitude affects pitch movement and strikeout rates.
Cold or hot affects velocity and grip.
Opener usage makes the listed pitcher's BF tiny or void.
Strikeout rungs share a latent mean and dispersion.
A plate-appearance simulation turns pitch cap, hook and per-PA K into a full strikeout distribution.

interactions.hypothesis: Pitch mix x lineup whiff by pitch: the strikeout rate is the usage-weighted sum of pitcher whiff and lineup whiff for each pitch type, not the product of aggregate K% rates.

Times-through-order x hook: the K rate decays by trip while the probability of reaching the third trip depends on pitch count and leash, so expected K is a sum over trips weighted by survival probabilities.

Umpire zone x called-strike rate: a larger zone helps pitchers who live on the edges (high called-strike rate), a smaller zone helps hitters, so the umpire effect should be scaled by the pitcher's edge-pitch share and catcher framing.
Pitch cap x efficiency x patience: outs scale with pitch cap divided by pitches per PA, which depends on the opposing lineup's patience, so the cap and lineup patience interact for outs markets.

mentions.target: Whether a specific word or phrase is spoken during a specified broadcast, per the contract's source and counting rules.
mentions.mechanism: Mentions depend on the announcers' vocabulary and on game events that trigger topics (milestones, pitching changes, weather), so the best-supported hypotheses concern crew habits, broadcast length and event likelihood; sports performance statistics have little direct predictive role. This is close to a novelty/language market with limited statistical structure and sparse history.

inputs.why: Crew language tendencies and base word rates.
Which crew and network call the game.
Storylines and events that trigger words.
Recent storylines or player news that announcers will discuss.
Weather delays add airtime and topics.
Longer games add airtime: from the tenth inning each half-inning starts with a runner on second (ghost runner), making extra innings short and shifting expectation of the winner.
Which feed, which speakers and spoken vs displayed words count.
Market-implied probability and its movement.
Historical realised frequency by word type.

interactions.hypothesis: Crew vocabulary x event triggers: the probability of a word equals baseline crew rate plus a trigger bump when the relevant event occurs, so event likelihood should be modelled separately.
Airtime length: delays and extra innings lengthen the broadcast, raising the chance of any word, so game-length uncertainty interacts with word rate.

awards_mkt.target: Winner or finalist of a league award (MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Manager of the Year, Gold Glove), as announced by the award body.
awards_mkt.mechanism: Voters choose from visible production and team narrative at a fixed time and with a specific ballot structure; the best model is a historical voter-behaviour model using WAR, counting stats and team success, updated by finalist announcements. Late-season results matter less if ballots are cast before the postseason.

inputs.why: Electorate, ballot structure and timing.
WAR and counting stats visible to voters.
Team success and storyline effects.
Leaderboard position in key stats.
Late-season injuries and games played.
Team playoff outcomes correlate with votes.
Projected final totals before voting closes.
Which award and which announcement defines settlement.
Information events around finalists.

interactions.hypothesis: Production rank x team success: voters weigh WAR with team record, so candidates on playoff teams gain relative to equal production on non-playoff teams.
Ballot timing x injuries: votes cast before the postseason make late-season results irrelevant, so injuries after the ballot deadline should not move the probability.

off_field.target: Non-game events (business, league announcements, non-baseball questions) settled by public announcement or defined sources.
off_field.mechanism: These markets depend on organisational decisions and external events rather than on-field performance. There is no strong statistical structure; value, if any, comes from reference-class frequencies, calendar constraints and timestamped news relative to the resolution wording. Many are effectively novelty markets with weak predictability from baseball data.

inputs.why: Reference-class frequency of similar events.
Timestamped news and reports: transactions and news change who plays and the team's strength with a lag before statistics catch up.
Transaction calendar where relevant.
Resolution wording and source.
Price reaction to news: the traded price aggregates every participant's information about this contract, including injury and lineup news that moves faster than public stats.
Liquidity affects quote reliability.
Close time vs event timing: market open, close, halts and postponement events determine when information can be traded on and which pregame snapshot is the last valid one.
Base rates by market type: realized frequency by rung gives the unconditional base rate that every conditional model must beat, and reveals persistent biases in how thresholds are set.

interactions.hypothesis: Base rate x time remaining: the hazard concentrates around known dates, so base rates must be time-conditioned by the market window.
News timing x resolution source: reports precede official announcements; the wording defines whether a report counts, so price reaction should be read against the rules.

transactions_mkt.target: Whether a transaction or personnel event occurs (trade, signing, call-up, manager/coach change, extension) by a given date.
transactions_mkt.mechanism: Transactions follow institutional calendars and team incentives: standing (buyer vs seller), contract status, roster rules and ownership/front-office behaviour. Reports from beat writers precede many moves. Probabilities are a hazard over the window, mostly estimated from reference classes with updates from reported news and standings.

inputs.why: Transaction timeline and rules.
Team standing drives trades: a team's playoff position and strategy determine whether it adds or sells players and thus the probability of a trade.
Option, 40-man and Rule 5 constraints.
Reports precede transactions: transactions and news change who plays and the team's strength with a lag before statistics catch up.
Injuries trigger call-ups and IL moves.
Playoff odds define buyer/seller state.
Reference-class frequencies: for off-field markets, history of similar announcements is the best available prior.
What counts as official transaction.
Market reaction to reports: the traded price aggregates every participant's information about this contract, including injury and lineup news that moves faster than public stats.

interactions.hypothesis: Playoff odds x contract status: sellers with expiring contracts are most likely traded, so standing and contract interact for trade-probability.
Rule calendar x report timing: option/40-man deadlines concentrate moves on certain dates, so hazards should be date-aware, and reports tighten the window.

season_outcome.target: Season-level outcomes: division winner, win totals, playoff qualification, pennant and championship futures, and postseason series.
season_outcome.mechanism: Futures integrate team talent (projections updated with run differential, not record) through the remaining schedule with uncertainty, then apply tiebreakers and the playoff bracket. Because talent uncertainty and injury information arrive slowly, prices depend on priors and on how fast they update; regressing sequencing luck is the central modelling choice.

inputs.why: Monte Carlo of the remaining schedule and bracket.
Talent prior from projection systems.
Regress luck in records: team records deviate from run-differential-based expectations because of sequencing, one-run games and bullpen luck, and deviations mean-revert.
Remaining schedule quality: future opponent quality, home/away split and days off shape expected wins for the remainder of the season.
Injuries to key players and depth.
Rotation quality especially for playoffs.
Bullpen quality in close games.
Seeding and tiebreaker rules: seeding, wild-card format and tiebreaker rules decide who plays whom and with what home field, determining futures settle paths.
Series state for postseason series.
Trades and call-ups: transactions and news change who plays and the team's strength with a lag before statistics catch up.
Futures benchmark: sharp sportsbook and exchange lines are a competing aggregation of information and the standard benchmark for fair probability.

interactions.hypothesis: Team talent uncertainty x short series: more uncertainty about true strength widens outcomes, and postseason rotations compress the talent gap, so pitching depth and rotation structure interact with series length.
Regress record luck x tiebreaker rules: with seeding contested, expected wins (not actual) feed the simulation but formal tiebreakers resolve the ties.
Injury state x remaining schedule: a long-term injury reduces strength for the remainder, with a larger effect when the remaining schedule is dense with strong opponents.

extras.target: Whether the game goes to extra innings (tied after nine), and related game-length outcomes.
extras.mechanism: Extra innings require a tie after nine innings; the probability is the probability that the two teams' run totals are equal, which is higher in low-scoring, close-spread games. The ghost-runner rule shortens extra innings but does not affect the event of reaching extras. Estimation requires a calibrated run distribution (with overdispersion and team correlation) and the contract's inclusion rule.

inputs.why: Tied-after-nine rate by total/spread bucket.
Distribution shape drives P(tie).
Strong starters lower totals and raise tie chance.
Late scoring quality: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Low-scoring parks tie more: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather shifts run scoring: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Offence quality sets run levels.
Rule for ghost runner: from the tenth inning each half-inning starts with a runner on second (ghost runner), making extra innings short and shifting expectation of the winner.

Wording for extras: the settlement wording defines which events count (overtime, extra innings, shootout goals, delayed games, DNPs) and therefore changes the true probability of the same real-world sport.

interactions.hypothesis: Low total x small spread: ties peak when both teams are expected to score little and are evenly matched, so the tie probability is a function of total and spread jointly.
Late-inning run scoring determines whether a tie at 9 persists; bullpen quality and manager decisions in innings 7-9 interact with starter exit.

first_inning_mkt.target: Whether a run is scored in the first inning (by either team or by a specific team), and first-inning run counts.
first_inning_mkt.mechanism: The first inning is the top three batters of each lineup against fresh starters, so the run probability is a function of those six hitters' on-base and power against the starting pitchers' first-trip profile, with park and weather scaling. The event is a union over two half-innings, each with roughly a modest probability, so the outcome is sensitive to the top-of-order quality and to the starter's early command; small samples make first-inning historical splits unreliable.

inputs.why: First-inning scoring distribution baseline.
Top-of-order quality vs starter.
Confirmed top three hitters: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Handedness matchup for the top of the order.
Starter first-trip performance.
Walk risk early: walks arise when pitchers miss the zone and hitters take pitches outside it; both the pitcher's command and the lineup's discipline matter.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Wind/temperature: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Zone effect in early innings: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
First-three-innings structure.
Rules for first-inning markets in shortened/postponed games.

interactions.hypothesis: Top-of-order OBP x starter command: the chance of a walk or hit by the first three batters scales with their OBP and the starter's zone rate, so the product (and the two-half-inning union) determines the event probability.
Starter first-trip profile x platoon: lefty-heavy top order against a righty with weak changeup raises first-inning scoring, so platoon should be applied at the top-three level.

delay.target: Whether a game is delayed (start delayed or play stopped for weather), postponed or suspended, per the contract definition.
delay.mechanism: Delay probability is a weather-timing problem: precipitation (or lightning) likelihood and intensity near first pitch relative to the roof status, and the decision behaviour of umpire crew and teams. It is largely independent of team quality; the information value is in forecast updates and in historical delay behaviour by park.

inputs.why: Historical delay rate and risk model.
Hourly precipitation probability and radar nowcast.
Lightning, wind and temperature.
Closed roof eliminates most delay risk.
Definitions of delay/suspend/postpone.
Doubleheaders and schedule flexibility affect postponement choices.
Contract's definition and time window.
Market close and actual first pitch timing.

interactions.hypothesis: Precipitation timing x roof status: the same forecast produces a delay only if the roof is open; roof state must gate the weather risk.
Definition of delay x time window: contracts counting only start delays are driven by pre-first-pitch weather while in-game delay contracts add game-length exposure.

player_hr.target: Whether a hitter hits at least one (or k) home run in the game, requiring appearance per the wording.
player_hr.mechanism: HR is a rare per-PA event whose probability is the hitter's HR rate (barrels, pull-air, FB%) modified by the pitcher's HR vulnerability, platoon, park HR factor by handedness and weather (wind, temperature), multiplied across expected PAs and hits against starter and bullpen. Variance is intrinsic; HR/FB luck regresses. Small multiplicative shifts in environment matter because of the low base probability.

inputs.why: Barrel%, pull-air and FB% predict HR beyond past HR.
Bat speed gives early power signal.
Pitcher's HR/FB and barrels allowed by hand.
Park HR factor by handedness and weather.
Wind component along pull-side field.
Air density and altitude: lower air density reduces drag and increases ball carry, raising HR and scoring (Denver, hot days).
Handedness matchup: same-handed matchups favour pitchers (especially vs breaking balls), opposite-handed matchups favour hitters, and the size of the split differs by player.
PA count multiplier: pA count is the volume multiplier for hits, TB, HR, RBI and runs, and depends on the lineup slot, the team's run environment and the opposing pitcher.
Regress HR/FB luck: home runs per fly ball regress strongly to a mean determined by park and contact quality, so past HR luck is not persistent.
Pitch-type matchup such as fastball hitters vs fastball-heavy pitchers.
Confirmed participation and slot.

interactions.hypothesis: Hitter pull-air x park pull-side HR factor x wind: HR probability depends on whether the hitter's fly balls go to the park's short side with wind, so these three need joint modelling.
Barrel rate x pitcher HR vulnerability: pitchers who throw center-cut fastballs raise HR chance most for hitters with high fastball barrel rates, so matchup beats aggregate rates.
PA count x per-PA HR: expected HR scales with plate appearances, so confirmed batting slot and team total directly shift the probability.

pitcher_er.target: Earned runs allowed by the starting pitcher in the game (threshold ladder).
pitcher_er.mechanism: Earned runs result from baserunners (hits, walks, HBP) and their conversion into runs given HR, sequencing and the bullpen's handling of inherited runners; they depend on batters faced (so on the hook) and per-PA run value. Luck components (BABIP, LOB%, HR/FB) are large, so skill-based estimators and regression matter; the right tail is driven by HR and by blow-up innings that also trigger early hooks.

inputs.why: Skill-based run-prevention estimate (SIERA/xFIP).
Batters faced determine exposure.
Early hook caps accumulating runs.
Lineup quality against the pitcher's handedness.
Confirmed lineup replaces probable.
Contact quality and defence: hits allowed depend on the quality of contact against a pitcher and the fielders converting it into outs.
HR risk drives earned runs: pitchers who allow fly balls and hard contact give up more home runs, and the hitter-pitcher combination determines the single-game probability.
Strand rate regression: runners stranded above or below the expected rate inflate or deflate ERA; strand rates regress strongly to the mean.
BABIP regression: batting average on balls in play deviates from what contact quality and defence imply, and the deviation mostly reverts.
Park run factors: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather scaling: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Zone effects: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Inherited runners charged to the starter.

Strand and BABIP luck: observed ER overstate or understate true run prevention; ER projections should use expected rates from K, BB, HR and contact quality.
Lineup strength x park/weather: runs scale non-linearly with offence in hitter-friendly environments, so lineup quality and park/wind interact.

pitcher_hits.target: Hits allowed by the starting pitcher in the game (threshold ladder).
pitcher_hits.mechanism: Hits allowed = balls in play x hit probability (a function of contact quality, defence, park and BABIP) plus home runs; K and BB rates determine how many batters put the ball in play. Variance is high and BABIP is mostly noise beyond contact quality, so expected-BABIP models and defence behind the pitcher are central; workload (batters faced) scales the total.

inputs.why: Contact allowed and fielding behind the pitcher.
Batters faced multiplier: batters faced is the volume multiplier for every pitcher counting stat (strikeouts, outs, hits, walks, earned runs) and sets how much bullpen exposure the game has.
Strikeouts remove balls in play.
Walks reduce balls in play: walks arise when pitchers miss the zone and hitters take pitches outside it; both the pitcher's command and the lineup's discipline matter.
Regress BABIP luck to expected.
Batted-ball mix influences hit types.
Starting defence in the confirmed lineup.
Lineup contact quality vs handedness.
Park hit factor: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.

Defence x ground-ball rate: infield defence quality matters more for ground-ball pitchers, so GB% interacts with team defence for hit probability.

pitcher_bb.target: Walks allowed by the starting pitcher in the game (threshold ladder).
pitcher_bb.mechanism: Walks = batters faced x per-PA BB probability, which combines the pitcher's command (zone rate, first-pitch strikes) with the lineup's patience and chase rates, modified by umpire zone and catcher framing. Counts are low and overdispersed, with intentional walks adding rare cases; workload and the hook matter, and walk-prone starters also tend to be pulled early.

Batters faced multiplier: batters faced is the volume multiplier for every pitcher counting stat (strikeouts, outs, hits, walks, earned runs) and sets how much bullpen exposure the game has.
Confirmed lineup patience: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Zone size changes ball/strike calls.
Receiving adds borderline strikes.
Patient lineups draw more walks.
Fatigue/injury effects on command.
Hook limits walks: managers remove starters based on pitch count, times through the order and leverage; leash determines batters faced and thus all pitcher counting stats.
Park and weather effects on grip/ball.
Weather effects on command: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Walk rungs consistency: rungs of a threshold ladder (e.g.

interactions.hypothesis: Pitcher zone rate x lineup chase rate: patient lineups walk more against pitchers who miss the zone, but chase-prone lineups reduce walks even against wild pitchers, so command and discipline interact.
Umpire zone x framing: small-zone umpires and weak framers raise walks, so the effect is larger for pitchers who rely on edge pitches.

lineup_role.target: Whether a player plays, starts or enters the game (participation markets), per the contract's definition.
lineup_role.mechanism: Participation is determined by manager decisions (rest days, platoon matchups), injury status and late scratches, and the lineup card posted a few hours before the game; before the card, probability is a function of rest-day patterns and matchup, after the card it is nearly certain except for in-game substitutions. The key is timing and the exact definition of 'play'.

inputs.why: Confirmed lineup card timing: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Starter/platoon/bench role: a player's role determines whether he starts and how many PAs he gets, which drives participation and counting-stat markets.
Rest after night games and travel.
IL status and scratches: absences change lineup/rotation composition and late scratches can void or reprice player markets.
Manager platoon style: managers differ in platoon usage and substitutions, affecting plate-appearance counts and which hitters face which pitchers.
Schedule density: fatigue and travel affect position players' availability, starters' rest and bullpen usage.
Beat-writer reports on availability.
Definition of playing and void rules.
Lineup posting vs market close.

interactions.hypothesis: Rest-day pattern x opposing handedness: platoon players sit against same-handed starters, so P(start) combines rest-day pattern and starter handedness.
Lineup posting time x market close: probabilities are mixtures until the card posts, so the card's timestamp relative to market close defines the information edge.

series_ctx.target: Postseason outcomes: winner of a playoff series or round, pennant or championship given the current bracket state.
series_ctx.mechanism: Series probability is a dynamic program over remaining games with per-game win probabilities that depend on announced starters, rest, bullpen availability, home-field pattern and injuries. Postseason managers shorten starter leash and use best relievers more, compressing talent gaps relative to the regular season, and rotation set by off-days matters more than ratings alone.

inputs.why: Series state, rest and rotation.
Elimination and leverage context.
Starters in the playoff rotation.
Shorter leash and high-leverage reliever usage.
Bullpen quality matters more in the postseason.
Offence vs likely starters: a team's lineup quality against the starter's handedness determines runs in the early innings, more than overall season team offence.
Key injuries before and during the series.
Home-field and bracket structure.
Talent prior: projection systems summarise multi-year talent estimates that are better priors for team strength than early-season results.

leaders.mechanism: Accumulated totals plus rest-of-season production determine the leader: projection = current total + rate x opportunity x availability. Rate stats require qualification; races depend on the top-tail distribution of contenders and on injuries. Because early-season leaders are driven by luck, rate regression to talent is the main lever.

inputs.why: Current leaderboard and games remaining.
Rate x opportunity projection.

True-talent rate for hitters: a hitter's quality per plate appearance (on-base skill, power, contact quality) determines hits, bases, runs and RBIs.

Special markets (e.g., records, league totals) depend on rate environments and the rule regime.

League-level rate environment.

League rate environment x team totals: a regime shift in run scoring moves all team run totals, so rule/ball regime interacts with run-total thresholds.

pitcher_strikeouts.label: Starting pitcher strikeouts thresholds
pitcher_strikeouts.target: Whether the listed starter records at least k strikeouts in the game (ladder of rungs), conditional on starting per the contract wording.
pitcher_strikeouts.mechanism: Expected strikeouts = expected batters faced x expected per-PA strikeout probability, summed over trips through the order. Per-PA K probability combines the pitcher's pitch-by-pitch swing-and-miss and called-strike skill (weighted by the pitch mix he uses against each batter handedness and in two-strike counts) with the confirmed lineup's whiff/K tendencies against those pitch types and handedness, then shifts with the umpire's zone, catcher framing, park/weather (velocity, movement) and the times-through-order penalty. Batters faced is capped by pitch count divided by pitches per PA and by the manager's hook, which depends on score, bullpen state and performance; realised pitch count is not knowable pregame, so the model is a mixture over exit scenarios and the outputs are a full count distribution, not a mean.

inputs.why: Baseline pitcher K%/CSW/whiff regressed and opposing lineup K% by handedness.
Pitch-by-pitch whiff and putaway rates by batter hand identify where Ks come from, and which pitches the starter will lean on.
Confirmed batting order's whiff rates against the pitcher's pitch types convert arsenal into a lineup-specific K expectation.
Confirmed-lineup K% against the pitcher's hand, weighted by PA slot, replaces team-average K%.
Usage by count and handedness, velocity and chase rates describe the mechanism and detect changes in arsenal.
Expected batters faced multiplies per-PA K probability; workload variance is often larger than rate uncertainty.
Run differential and pitch count drive the early hook that truncates strikeout opportunity.
Returning-from-injury or workload caps create a hard ceiling on batters faced.
Pitches per PA convert pitch cap into batters faced; strikeouts cost extra pitches.
Patient lineups run up pitch counts and may shorten outings while whiffing less on pitches out of the zone.
Third-time-through penalty reduces per-PA K and raises hook probability late in the outing.
Umpire's called-strike zone shifts K and BB probabilities for the game.
Umpire K%/BB% over expected adjusted for pitcher/batter mix gives magnitude for the zone effect.
Catcher receiving changes called-strike rate on borderline pitches; backup catchers alter the environment.
Velocity or spin decline flags fatigue or injury and predicts lower whiff and earlier exit.
Opener/bullpen game flags make the listed pitcher's batters faced tiny or the market void.
Bullpen availability and fatigue change how long the manager lets the starter go.
Park and altitude influence pitch movement and K rates modestly and pitch count via run environment.
Cold weather lowers velocity and spin, hot weather helps contact carry; effect on whiff is small but plausible.
Handedness composition of the lineup (and switch hitters) determines which pitch types are effective.
Late scratches in the lineup change the K mix; pitcher scratch voids or reprices the market.
Strikeout rungs must imply a coherent distribution; stale rungs after lineup news can be detected.
Settlement wording on starter requirement, innings and voids.
Price move after lineup confirmation and umpire assignment reveals how the market incorporated the news.

Strikeout rungs at 8+ to 10+ are sensitive to which sub-event drives a pitcher's K%, and a lineup of patient fouling hitters is a different test than a lineup of free swingers; this keeps the matchup count-state-aware.

The Kalshi ladder pays on the right tail of strikeouts, and the right tail is exit-time driven; a hazard curve makes the hook policy of this manager and this bullpen state an explicit, testable factor.
Rungs are nested thresholds on one count; without the dispersion parameter the model cannot price both tails of the ladder consistently.
A backup catcher can shift the called-strike share enough to move a 7+/8+ rung, and the information arrives with the lineup.
Adds the missing 2026+ zone mechanism for strikeout ladders, where called third strikes and count leverage are central.

interactions.hypothesis: Pitch mix x lineup whiff by pitch: K rate = sum over pitch types of usage x pitcher whiff x lineup whiff relative to league on that pitch; a slider-heavy pitcher against a lineup weak vs sliders is worth more than aggregate K% suggests.

Times-through-order x hook: K per BF declines each trip while survival to later trips depends on pitch count and leash, so expected K is a survival-weighted sum across trips and a short leash cuts the high-K tail.

Umpire zone x called-strike rate x framing: a wide zone adds called strikes mainly for pitchers who work the edges and with strong framing, so the umpire adjustment should be scaled by the pitcher's edge/called-strike share.

Platoon x pitch mix x confirmed lineup: lineup handedness determines whether the changeup (vs opposite-hand) or the breaking ball (vs same-hand) is used, so lineup handedness composition shifts the pitch mix, and hence K%.

Pitch cap x efficiency x opponent patience: batters faced = cap / pitches per PA, where P/PA depends on both pitcher efficiency and lineup patience, so cap and patience must be modelled jointly (and a high-K strategy is pitch-expensive).
Velocity trend x leash: a pitcher with falling velocity gets pulled earlier by performance, so velocity signals should adjust both per-PA K and exit probability.

A high-strikeout style raises the number of two-strike pitches and fouls, so the same pitcher who gains Ks per batter also spends more pitches per batter and survives fewer batters. Strikeouts and batters faced are therefore negatively coupled through the pitch budget, and the coupling is strongest against patient lineups that foul off two-strike pitches.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit K and BF jointly (copula or simulation) versus independent product; compare tail calibration of 8+/9+ rungs for high-whiff pitchers against patient lineups.

interactions.hypothesis: The contract settles an opener on the small count but settles a scratch at the undefined fair market price, so the distribution is a mixture over three regimes whose weights move with news. The hazard curve differs by regime (about 3-4 batters for an opener versus a normal starter curve), and the mixture weight, not the performance model, dominates high-rung probability whenever opener risk is above a few percent.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare model log loss on starts flagged opener-risk versus not; test whether adding a regime indicator removes miscalibration at 7+ rungs.

interactions.hypothesis: Called strikes contribute only to the looking-strikeout share of a pitcher's Ks, so a wider zone and a better framer help most the pitchers who live on the edges and hurt least those who get strikeouts swinging. Adjustments must be scaled by the pitcher's looking-K share rather than added flat. Under the 2026 ABS challenge regime the zone effect is partially overridden on challenged edge pitches, so the interaction must be estimated with a regime flag and shrunk umpire/framing coefficients.
interactions.how_to_test: Add terms umpire_effect x looking_K_share and framing x edge_pitch_share; check coefficient sign and out-of-sample gain.

interactions.hypothesis: On the second and third trips pitchers lean away from their best pitch and hitters have seen it, so the effective whiff rate steps down at batter 19 and 28 while lineup whiff by pitch type changes sign of importance (the offspeed whiff matters more later). The decay is a step at trip boundaries, not smooth in batters faced.
interactions.how_to_test: Include trip-indexed pitch-mix usage and trip dummies; test slope discontinuity at BF 18/27 in per-batter K logistic.

interactions.hypothesis: Start-level latent quality widens the K distribution as batters faced grows (variance of a correlated sum scales with BF squared), so on long outings a good day produces 11+ Ks far more often than independence implies. Early velocity relative to baseline is the only pregame-adjacent signal of the latent state.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate rho by BF bucket and by first-inning velocity deviation (post-hoc check); compare rung calibration with and without the rho term.

nonlinearities.shape: S-shaped threshold in batters faced: P(K>=k) rises steeply across the BF range where k/K% falls (about 27-33 BF for a 9+ rung at 30% K), nearly zero below 20 BF and saturating above 33
nonlinearities.why: Strikeouts are bounded by batters faced, so rung probabilities are a steep logistic in BF near the rung's requirement and flat elsewhere; linear workload terms mis-price the middle rungs.

nonlinearities.shape: Approximate step or steep gradient around the second and third trips (batters 18-19 and 27-28); exact form is uncertain (see ks_shape_constants)
nonlinearities.why: Times-through-the-order penalties and the managerial gate act at trip boundaries; a smooth innings term spreads a discrete change and hides the hook cliff.

nonlinearities.shape: Assumed threshold: little effect for small velocity drops and a sharp negative effect for sustained larger drops; the 1 mph cutoff is an unsourced guess to be estimated
nonlinearities.why: Velocity noise start to start is large; only a sustained multi-start decline separates a sick arm, so a linear velocity term is dominated by noise.

nonlinearities.shape: Odds-ratio (log5-type) combination rather than additive; saturating at extreme pitcher K% against high-whiff lineups
nonlinearities.why: Per-batter K probability combines pitcher and batter propensities multiplicatively on the odds scale, so adding K% differences over-predicts at the extremes.

mechanism_review.summary: A starter's strikeout total is a compound count: the number of batters he faces times a per-batter strikeout probability that is re-drawn at every plate appearance. Batters faced is itself the outcome of three competing stopping rules: a pitch budget (rehab or season cap), a performance hook (runs and baserunners allowed trigger a pull), and a managerial inning/trip-through-the-order gate. The per-batter probability comes from the pitcher's pitch-type whiff and called-strike skill applied to the specific nine hitters, their handedness, their whiff by pitch type, and the count dynamics (how often a PA reaches two strikes and how often a two-strike PA ends in K). Umpire zone, catcher and park shift it at the margin. The two pieces are negatively coupled through pitch cost (a strikeout takes more pitches than a ground out) and positively coupled through shared latent 'stuff day' quality, so the output is a joint distribution, with rung probabilities set by the right tail of batters faced multiplied by an overdispersed K-per-batter law. Because Kalshi settles non-starts at an undefined fair market price but settles injury exits and openers on the small count, the start-confirmation stage creates a conditional mixture that must be modelled separately from pure performance.

stages.name: Start status and role gate
stages.description: Before anything else the pitcher must be the listed starter. A scratch settles at the undefined 'fair market price', so it changes holders' P&L and is a priced state rather than a state outside the payoff, but an opener or a short-bulk plan means the pitcher starts, faces three or four batters and settles on a tiny count. The gate therefore has three regimes (conventional starter, planned short outing, non-start) and everything downstream is a mixture over regimes weighted by the probability each regime is true at the time the market is traded, which changes when the lineup card and probable-pitcher updates post.
stages.distribution: Discrete 3-regime categorical; regime probabilities move from near-prior (days before) to near 0/1 at lineup posting. Heavy mass at 'conventional' for most rotation starters, rare but extreme opener regime.

stages.name: Batters-faced budget and hook hazard
stages.description: Given a conventional start, the exit point is a first-passage time: each batter faced carries a hazard of removal that depends on cumulative pitch count, trip through the order, runs and baserunners allowed so far, bullpen freshness and the specific manager's policy. The pitch budget (return from injury, workload cap) is a hard ceiling that truncates the right tail. Because K rungs sit in the right tail (8+, 9+, 10+), what matters is not the mean innings but the probability of surviving to 25-30 batters faced.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed, truncated discrete (about 12-30 batters faced) with a point mass at the cap and a left tail of early blow-up exits; start-to-start variance larger than rate uncertainty.

stages.name: Per-batter strikeout probability
stages.description: Within a PA the strikeout is a sequence: reach two strikes, then convert a two-strike count with a swing-and-miss, a called third strike or a foul tip. The pitcher's arsenal (usage by count and batter hand, whiff and chase by pitch) meets each batter's whiff and chase profile by pitch type; the odds-ratio combination of two rates is not additive. The confirmed lineup order matters because the nine hitters are not interchangeable and the top of the order is seen more often when the pitcher goes deep. Times-through-the-order decay lowers the rate on trips two and three.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli per batter with probability roughly 0.15 to 0.40 depending on matchup; heterogeneity across the nine batters creates a Poisson-binomial rather than a binomial count.

stages.name: Zone regime (ABS challenges), catcher and environment shifts
stages.description: The home-plate umpire's called zone and the catcher's receiving change the share of borderline pitches called strikes, which converts to strike-three-looking events and to count leverage on every PA; cold air and altitude change spin and movement slightly. These shifts are small relative to the matchup but are known only late (umpire and catcher assignments), so they are timing-sensitive adjustments applied on top of s3. Since 2026 MLB uses the ABS challenge system in all regular-season and postseason games (two challenges per team, borderline pitches reviewed by the automated zone), so human-umpire zone and catcher framing history (UmpScorecards, framing runs) comes from a different regime; framing and umpire effects are shrunk harder toward neutral for 2026+ and the challenge-usage and success pattern becomes an input.
stages.distribution: Small multiplicative shift on per-batter K probability (a few percent of rate); effect heterogeneous by pitcher's looking-strikeout share.

stages.name: Count distribution and start-level latent state
stages.description: Realised strikeouts vary more than a binomial with the right mean because pitchers have good and bad days that move whiff rate for all batters at once (grip, command, release), and because K and batters faced are coupled by pitch cost. The settled probability of each rung is the upper tail of this overdispersed, coupled distribution, and neighbouring rungs are nested so a single latent explains the whole ladder.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed count (Beta-binomial-like) with positive within-start correlation and negative K-vs-BF coupling via pitch cost; fat right tail relative to binomial.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Yes if the named starting pitcher is credited with at least N strikeouts in the one listed game (ladder of 'N+' rungs, one market per N). The pitcher must be the game's starting pitcher and face at least one batter; if he is scratched or is not a starter the market pays the fair market price (a settlement at an undefined 'fair market price', not a No and not necessarily a refund at the entry price; see ks_fair_price_definition); relief appearances never count even if the same man enters later. Strikeouts are the official-scorer count for that pitcher (a strike three that is dropped and lets the batter reach still counts for the pitcher). The sampled text is silent on postponement/suspension and names no explicit data source.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official MLB box score / play-by-play strikeouts for the pitcher (MLB Stats API gamefeed or Retrosheet-equivalent). The sampled rules do not name the source, so this is the presumed source of truth.
variants_and_edge_cases: Opener or bulk-guy usage: an opener who starts and faces 3-4 batters is still 'a starting pitcher with a batter faced', so the market settles No on 5+/6+ rungs rather than voiding; the 'bulk' reliever who follows is excluded by the relief rule.

Settlement asymmetry: a scratch or a non-start settles at the undefined 'fair market price' (a priced settlement value, not a refund at entry and not a No), but an in-game injury after one batter faced settles on whatever count exists, so injury-exit risk is a priced tail, not a void.

Postponement, suspension, rain-shortened games and extra innings are not addressed in the sampled rules_secondary (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS); a rain-shortened start that reaches few innings still settles on the count recorded.
Counting rule: only strikeouts charged to this pitcher count; dropped-third-strike and strikeout-throw-out plays follow official scoring; Postseason games use the same ladder with shorter hooks.

Zero-batter starter is undefined by the sampled text: the rule covers a starter with at least one batter faced and a scratch or non-starter, but not a starter who throws pitches and leaves (injury, ejection, rain) before a batter is faced (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS, see ks_zero_batter_starter).

pitcher_outs.label: Starting pitcher outs recorded (innings pitched) thresholds
pitcher_outs.target: Whether the starter records at least k outs (e.g. 15 outs = five innings), requiring the pitcher to start per the wording.
pitcher_outs.mechanism: Outs = batters faced x probability each PA ends in at least one out, so the outcome is the workload distribution times (1 - on-base rate allowed) and is capped by the pitch limit and the manager's hook. Unlike strikeouts, outs are highly sensitive to run prevention in-game (a bad inning triggers an early pull) and to pitcher efficiency (pitches per out), so the distribution is left-skewed with a mass of early exits and a ceiling near the cap. The key information is pitch cap, hook policy, run-prevention quality and the opponent's on-base skills; realised pitch count is unknown before the game.

inputs.why: Expected batters faced/pitch count distribution is the primary driver of outs.
Manager hook tendencies and score/bullpen contingencies determine early-exit probability.
Rehab, return and workload caps create hard ceilings on outs.
Pitches per out (low P/PA, high first-pitch strike) lets pitchers record more outs per 100 pitches.
Patient lineups raise pitches per out.
Run-prevention quality lowers blow-up risk that triggers early hooks.
Contact allowed and defence drive on-base events per BF.
Walks are pitch-expensive non-outs.
Strikeouts are outs but cost pitches; interplay with efficiency.
Third-trip penalty raises on-base rate and pull probability.
Velocity loss predicts shorter outing.
Rest and last start's pitch count affect stamina and cap.
Short or tired bullpen lengthens the leash; fresh bullpen shortens it.
Openers and bullpen games make the listed pitcher's outs very small.
Postseason hooks are shorter, moving outs distribution.
Heat and delays affect stamina and manager decisions.
Run environment influences blow-up risk.
Starter requirement and handling of partial innings, delays and voids.
Outs rungs at 15/18/21 outs are strongly nested and share a workload latent.
The ladder is lattice-valued; managers' inning-completion habits decide whether neighbouring rungs are priced near-equal or far apart.
Directly converts the batters-faced distribution into outs; a pitcher with 24 BF and 4 DP outs gets 3 more outs than 'one out per out-batter' implies.
Rain is the one interruption that changes outs without any pitching information.
Supplies the opposing-offence driver of outs per batter faced, which the pitcher-only inputs lacked.
Replaces the circular claim that the zone effect is already inside pitches per PA by modelling the 2026 regime shift explicitly.

interactions.hypothesis: Pitch cap x pitches per out: the ceiling on outs is cap divided by pitches per out, so the cap and efficiency (and opponent patience) interact and determine the upper tail.
Performance-triggered hook: early runs and baserunners trigger pulls, so run-prevention quality, contact allowed and manager hook policy interact to create the left tail of outs.
Bullpen state x leash: a depleted bullpen lengthens the starter's leash while a rested bullpen and analytics-driven manager shorten it before the third trip.
Opener flag x listed pitcher: opener usage collapses outs (and may void), so probable-pitcher status must gate every other input.

The outs ceiling equals the pitch cap divided by pitches per out, so for capped starters (rehab, innings limit) the cap is binding and the opponent's patience determines which rung the ceiling falls on; for uncapped starters the cap never binds and patience only matters through the performance hook. The effect is a regime switch on whether cap/(pitches per out) falls below the rung.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute cap-implied outs ceiling per start and compare tail calibration for capped versus uncapped starts.

interactions.hypothesis: Managers who pull at the start of the third trip remove starters at outs 18 and nearly never at 19-20, while fresh bullpens raise the probability a hook is pulled at the boundary. The rung P(outs>=19) therefore depends on the boundary decision rather than on running performance, and the dependence is on the bullpen state in discrete steps.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate exit mass at j=18 by bullpen-freshness tercile and by manager; check discontinuity of P(outs>=18) vs P(outs>=19).

interactions.hypothesis: Early runs convert contact allowed into a pull: a starter with weak contact suppression who allows a first-inning crooked number is removed early, so the same quality gap shows up as a left-tail mass rather than a shift of the mean. The hook response is conditional on runs allowed to date, not on pregame quality alone.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit hazard with runs-allowed interaction by pitcher contact-quality tercile on historical starts; compare predicted P(outs<=9) to observed.

interactions.hypothesis: Ground-ball pitchers earn extra outs by double plays when a runner is on first, but only in lineups that put runners on and hit grounders; strikeout pitchers earn no DP outs. Outs per BF is therefore a product of GB share, traffic on first and lineup DP rate rather than an additive pitcher quality term.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare outs-per-BF prediction with and without the GB x traffic x DP-rate term on held-out starts.

interactions.hypothesis: A weather delay matters only when the roof is open and rain overlaps the middle innings; given a delay over an hour the starter usually does not return, so the effect on outs is conditional on both timing and length, truncating the right tail only in wet parks.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition outs distribution on delayed-game flag in historical data by park roof type; estimate fraction of delayed games where the starter returns.

interactions.hypothesis: Outs recorded are pitch budget divided by pitches per out, and pitches per out is pitches per PA divided by outs per PA: a lineup with low out rate raises pitches per out and pulls the pitch ceiling down, so lineup out-rate and pitch efficiency multiply through the cap rather than adding.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress outs recorded on pitch budget / (pitches per PA / lineup outs per PA) and compare with additive terms across starts with announced caps.

nonlinearities.shape: Hard ceiling: probability mass piled at cap/pitches-per-out, none above
nonlinearities.why: A cap truncates outs sharply; a linear effect of the cap smears out a point mass and mis-prices the rung that sits exactly at the ceiling.

nonlinearities.shape: Lumpy lattice: spikes at multiples of three outs (inning ends) and at third-trip start
nonlinearities.why: Removals cluster at inning boundaries, so the survival function falls in steps; a smooth hazard in outs gives the wrong rung spacing.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex cost: pitches per PA above about 4.2 compounds through full counts and long at-bats, shortening outings disproportionately
nonlinearities.why: A few high-leverage two-strike battles make pitch spending right-skewed, so average pitches per PA understates the probability of a high-pitch-count outing.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold at sustained multi-start decline; flat inside normal start-to-start noise
nonlinearities.why: Only a decline outside noise predicts injury or fatigue exits; before that velocity is uninformative about outs.

mechanism_review.summary: Outs recorded by a starter is a first-passage quantity: the game removes the pitcher at a stopping time and the count at that time is outs. Each plate appearance produces one out with a probability that is not simply one minus on-base percentage, because ground-ball double plays add a second out on the same batter, and caught stealings and pickoffs add outs without a plate appearance. The stopping time is set by a pitch budget (cap or workload ramp), by pitch cost per out (strikeouts and walks are expensive, early-count ground balls are cheap), by a performance trigger (runs and traffic cause a pull), and by managerial exit conventions that concentrate removals at inning ends and at the start of the third trip through the order. The right tail is bounded by the pitch ceiling divided by pitches per out and the left tail by blow-ups, giving a left-skewed, lumpy distribution on a lattice of thirds of innings. Rung probabilities near multiples of three depend on exit-boundary behaviour as much as on pitcher quality, and rain delays and openers act as regime switches.

stages.name: Starter identity and one-pitch gate
stages.description: The pitcher must be the starter; openers and bulk-guy plans collapse outs to roughly three to six, while a conventional starter is on a 15-21 out scale. Under the KXMLBOUTS wording the gate is one pitch, so an early injury also settles low rather than at the fair market price. The stage therefore yields a regime probability (conventional, opener, bulk-after-opener, non-start) that must be combined with the performance model, and the regime posterior changes at the lineup card and at warm-up reports.
stages.distribution: Categorical with a rare, extreme opener regime; regime posterior is a step function in time around lineup posting.

stages.name: Pitch budget and cost per out
stages.description: The ceiling on outs is the pitch cap divided by pitches per out. Pitches per out equals pitches per plate appearance divided by outs per plate appearance, so a pitcher with good pitches-per-PA but a high on-base rate against may still be pitch-inefficient, and a patient lineup lifts pitches per PA and shortens the outing before performance does. Return-from-injury caps, season innings limits and days of rest set the cap itself, which is often announced rather than inferred.
stages.distribution: Truncated right tail with a point mass at the cap (about 85-110 pitches); pitches per out roughly 5-7, right-skewed by long at-bats.

stages.name: Outs generated per batter and on the bases
stages.description: Outs per batter faced is one minus the rate of reaching base (hits, walks, hit by pitch, reach on error) plus extra outs from double plays and baserunning outs. Strikeouts and ground balls convert at different pitch costs: strikeouts generate an out with certainty only when the batter does not reach on a dropped third strike, ground balls add double-play upside when a runner is on first. The lineup's on-base and double-play proneness and the defense behind the pitcher decide how many outs arrive per hundred pitches.
stages.distribution: Per-batter near-Bernoulli (out probability about 0.68-0.78) with an upside tail from double plays; baserunning outs are rare, independent Poisson-like.

stages.name: Performance trigger and exit-boundary policy
stages.description: A starter is removed when a hook rule fires: a bad inning with runs and runners, the third time through the order, a pitch count threshold, or simply an inning end. Managers differ in whether they let a starter finish an inning, and removals concentrate on inning boundaries and at the first batter of the third trip, so the exit-out distribution has mass spikes at multiples of three. Bullpen freshness and series position (postseason leash) shift the probabilities.
stages.distribution: Lattice-valued exit time with spikes at outs divisible by 3, left tail of blow-up exits, ceiling exits; mixture over managers.

stages.name: Weather and delay interruptions
stages.description: A rain delay of an hour or more ends most starters' nights, so outs freeze at the delay point; heat and humidity affect pitch count tolerance at the margin. The probability of an in-game delay depends on the forecast and roof status, and the removal-after-delay behaviour is a separate manager policy.
stages.distribution: Rare discrete truncation event (delay probability a few percent, higher in rain-prone parks) with near-certain removal conditional on a long delay.

talent_strength.note: Run-prevention quality lowers blow-up exits.

opponent_matchup.note: Patience and contact of the lineup.

environment.note: Heat, park, delay interruption.

pace_volume.note: Pitch budget and cost per out.

efficiency_conversion.note: Outs per batter incl. DP/baserunning.

distribution_variance.note: Lattice with exit spikes.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest days and workload.

officiating_rules.note: 2026 ABS challenges change walks and pitch cost per out; modelled through abs_zone_pitch_cost.

settlement_contract.note: The one-pitch gate, fair-market-price settlement of scratches and the relief exclusion are quoted verbatim from KXMLBOUTS in rules_evidence.

contract_review.settlement_definition: KXMLBOUTS (the only live series, now filed in this archetype) pays Yes if the named starting pitcher records at least N outs in the listed game ('15+' rung, floor_strike 14.5 sampled). Gate: 'If Drew Rasmussen is a starting pitcher and records at least one pitch the market will settle based on outs recorded', i.e. one pitch thrown, not one batter faced as in the strikeout, earned-run and walk ladders. A scratch or non-starter settles at the undefined 'fair market price' (not a refund at entry), and a later relief appearance does not count. Outs are presumed to be the official-scorer outs credited while he is on the mound (thirds of an inning). Postponement, suspension and shortened-game handling are not stated and no data source is named.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box-score outs / innings pitched for the starter (MLB Stats API or Retrosheet); presumed, because the KXMLBOUTS text names no source.
variants_and_edge_cases: Gate difference versus the strikeout ladder: KXMLBOUTS triggers on one pitch thrown (not one batter faced), so a starter injured on his first pitch settles on zero outs (a No for every rung) rather than at the fair market price.

Outs are not innings: partial innings count and outs recorded by double plays, caught-stealing and pickoffs are presumed (box-score convention, not rules text) to count for the pitcher on the mound; only the 15+ rung (floor_strike 14.5) was sampled, so the existence of other rungs is not established.
Rain delay or suspension during the start: the starter may be removed after a long delay and the count freezes; postponement treatment is CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS in the sampled text.

Rung construction is an 'N+' ladder (the sampled rung 15+ equals five full innings); if rungs at multiples of three or at 16 and 17 exist (not sampled), boundaries sit where managerial exits cluster, which would make adjacent rungs differ by more than a smooth model implies.

pitcher_earned_runs_hits_walks.label: Starting pitcher earned runs, hits allowed and walks allowed
pitcher_earned_runs_hits_walks.target: Whether the starter allows at least k earned runs, hits or walks in the game, requiring the pitcher to start per the wording.
pitcher_earned_runs_hits_walks.mechanism: All three are batters faced times a per-PA event rate, but with different structure: hits depend on contact quality, defence and BABIP luck with K and BB removing balls in play; walks depend on the pitcher's command versus the lineup's patience and on the umpire zone and framing; earned runs add sequencing (LOB%, HR) on top of baserunners and truncate with the hook. The three are positively correlated within a start through shared latent command and contact quality and negatively with outs/strikeouts. Luck components (BABIP, LOB%, HR/FB) are large and regress, so expected-rate models beat observed outcomes.

inputs.why: Batters faced multiplier for all three stats.
Exit time bounds the number of batters faced and therefore every count stat.
Contact quality allowed and defence behind the pitcher drive hits and runs.
Pitcher command vs lineup chase and walk rates drive walks.
Lineup quality vs pitcher's handedness for hits and runs.
Confirmed lineup replaces probable lineups.
HR risk is the biggest driver of earned run tails.
Regress BABIP to expected for hits.
Regress strand rate for earned runs.
Umpire zone changes walks and runs.
Framing affects walks: a catcher who gets more borderline pitches called strikes raises the pitcher's strikeout and lowers walk rates.
Strikeouts remove baserunner chances.
Ground-ball pitchers allow fewer extra-base hits.
Fielders convert balls in play to outs.
Park run and hit factors: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather and wind shift hits and HR.
Inherited runners charged to the starter depend on bullpen.
Starter requirement, definitions of earned runs and scoring changes.
Threshold rungs for the three stats are internally nested.
A plate-appearance simulation produces the full distribution of hits, walks and earned runs from matchup probabilities.
Counts are over-dispersed; ignoring that mis-prices the tails of ladder thresholds.
Provides the conversion from hits and walks ladders to the earned-runs ladder without relying on a regressed LOB% alone.

Earned runs ladder differs from the runs distribution by this share; rungs at 3+ and 4+ move materially on a bad defense. Category reflects a fielding/defence quantity (errors and passed balls) rather than an official judgement, though the earned/unearned split is an official-scorer rule.
Needed for the ER tail rungs where blow-ups leave a crowded base path.
Hits allowed is a scorer-decided count; tendencies shift rungs slightly and can flip close settlements.
Adds the missing 2026 zone-regime driver to the walks ladder and to baserunner volume for ER.

interactions.hypothesis: Hits = balls in play x hit rate: K% and BB% determine balls in play, contact quality and defence determine conversion, so strikeout and contact profiles must be combined, not treated as independent.
Walks: pitcher zone rate x lineup chase/patience x umpire zone x framing; each is modest but together can move walk probability materially for command-poor pitchers.
Earned-run tail: HR vulnerability x park/wind x hook; early HR-driven blow-ups cause pulls, truncating but fattening the middle of the distribution.
Luck regression: observed BABIP and LOB% revert, so expected hits and earned runs use xBABIP and FIP-style run estimators with sample-weighted shrinkage.

Hits equal balls in play times hit probability, and balls in play are batters faced minus strikeouts, walks and home runs. A high-strikeout pitcher therefore has lower exposure to BABIP luck and a pitcher with a high BABIP-against can still be low on hits if he strikes batters out, so the effect of contact quality is scaled by the share of PAs that reach play.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress hits on BIP count and BABIP-expected separately versus on batters faced; check which has lower residual overdispersion.

interactions.hypothesis: Walk probability per PA rises convexly with the number of borderline balls called, because full counts compound: a smaller called zone and a poor framer push more counts to 3-ball, and each added ball increases the chance of a walk non-linearly. Command-poor pitchers against patient lineups are most exposed. In 2026 the zone is partly overridden by ABS challenges, so umpire and framing coefficients are estimated with a regime flag.
interactions.how_to_test: Add zone-size x pitcher edge rate x lineup chase interaction in a count-level walk model; test convexity in the zone-size term.

interactions.hypothesis: A home run costs one run plus the number of runners aboard, so expected earned runs from HR vulnerability grows convexly with traffic; HR-friendly parks and wind raise the probability that traffic is cleared. The ER ladder at 4+ is dominated by this joint of traffic and HR, not by average HR rate.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute expected ER from base-out Markov with HR probability by state versus flat HR/9; compare calibration of 4+ ER rung.

interactions.hypothesis: If the starter is pulled with runners on base, part of his final earned runs depends on which reliever enters and how fresh the bullpen is. The hook and the bullpen jointly create a conditional addition to ER that is largest in exactly the outings that already ended badly.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition ER residual on exit-with-traffic flag and reliever quality tercile; estimate added runs per inherited runner.

interactions.hypothesis: When an error or passed ball extends an inning, the scorer reconstructs the inning and later runs become unearned, so ER switches regime from tracking runs to lagging them. Teams with weak infield defense or a passed-ball catcher spend more time in the second regime.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare model fit predicting ER vs predicting runs and applying team-level unearned share; test whether team error rate improves ER calibration.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold in batters faced for ER and hits rungs (4+ ER nearly impossible under about 15 BF, hits 7+ needs about 24+ BF)
nonlinearities.why: Counts of hits and runs are bounded by exposure; rung probabilities are steep logistic functions of batters faced near the rung requirement.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex: HR rate effect on ER grows with traffic (ER gain per extra HR is not constant)
nonlinearities.why: A home run is worth more with runners aboard, so HR tendency interacts with baserunner volume and the ER ladder's right tail steepens.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in zone rate (cutoff near 42 percent is an unsourced author guess to be estimated); ABS regime shifts the curve
nonlinearities.why: Count leverage compounds through three-ball counts, so a small drop in strike rate produces an accelerating increase in walks.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating regression: extreme LOB% deviations (>80% or <65%) revert more than linear
nonlinearities.why: Strand luck is bounded by baserunner volume and pitcher skill; extremes carry less persistent information than a linear coefficient implies.

mechanism_review.summary: Hits, walks and earned runs allowed by a starter are three linked counts generated by the same sequence of batters faced but with different branching structure. Batters faced is truncated by the hook. Each batter ends in a strikeout, a walk or hit-by-pitch, a ball in play, or a home run. Walks come from command against plate discipline and the called zone; hits come from balls in play multiplied by hit probability set by contact quality, defense, park and luck; earned runs are a downstream function of how baserunners are sequenced by extra-base hits and home runs, how many are stranded, how many runs are charged as unearned, and how many inherited runners the bullpen lets score after exit. The three counts share latent command and contact quality, so they are positively correlated, and they are negatively correlated with outs and strikeouts. Because earned runs truncate the outing (a blow-up ends it), the ER distribution is a mixture of normal outings and early-exit blow-ups with a heavy right tail only partly capped. Hits and walks are close to compound-binomial in batters faced, while earned runs need base-out state.

stages.name: Gate and exposure
stages.description: The starter must have faced a batter. Exposure is batters faced from the hook process, the same stopping-time logic that governs outs but here with an asymmetry: runs allowed accelerate the pull, so the number of batters faced is endogenous to the counts being predicted, which truncates the ER tail and the hits tail in blow-up games.
stages.distribution: Truncated discrete exposure correlated with the outcomes themselves.

stages.name: Plate-appearance outcome split
stages.description: For each batter the outcome is a multinomial among strikeout, walk or HBP, ball in play, and home run. Strikeout and walk rates come from the pitcher's strike-throwing and the lineup's chase and patience; the batted-ball mix (ground, line, fly) is set by pitcher profile and hitters' swing. Each branch uses an odds-ratio combination of pitcher and batter skill, then is adjusted for platoon, park, umpire and catcher receiving.
stages.distribution: Multinomial per batter; heterogeneity across the lineup makes counts Poisson-binomial; HBP is rare.

stages.name: Balls in play to hits
stages.description: Hits equal balls in play times the probability a ball in play is a hit, which depends on exit velocity and angle mix (expected batting average on contact), defense and positioning, park dimensions and surface, and luck that regresses. High-strikeout pitchers face fewer balls in play, so hits are mechanically coupled to strikeouts and walks through the balls-in-play count. The official scorer's hit-versus-error call is the final filter.
stages.distribution: Binomial in balls in play with overdispersion from batted-ball quality clustering; scorer discretion adds a small noise term.

stages.name: Baserunner sequencing to earned runs
stages.description: Runs depend on the base-out states hits and walks create, on extra-base hits and home runs that advance runners, and on stranding. Home runs score the batter plus every runner, so traffic multiplies HR cost; errors and passed balls produce unearned runs that are not charged. Inherited runners left by the starter add charged runs after exit. A base-out run-expectancy conversion of baserunners is a better predictor than LOB% regression.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed count with zero mass (about 35-40% of starts allow 0-1 ER) and a heavy right tail from HR plus traffic; truncated by the hook.

stages.name: Joint distribution across the three ladders
stages.description: The three counts share start-level latent command (pitch location, release) and contact quality, so they are correlated within a start, while rungs within each ladder are nested events of one count. Pricing consistency across H, BB and ER ladders requires the joint distribution, not three independent marginals, and plate-appearance simulation generates it naturally.
stages.distribution: Positively correlated overdispersed counts (H, BB, ER) with negative correlation to K and outs; copula-like dependence.
