contract_review.settlement_definition: Three starter ladders now filed here, all with sampled rules: KXMLBERA (earned runs), KXMLBWA (walks allowed) and KXMLBHA (hits allowed) pay Yes if the named starter 'records N+' of the stat in the listed game. All three use the same gate: a starter with 'at least one batter faced' settles on the recorded count; a scratch or non-starter settles at the undefined 'fair market price'; relief appearances are excluded. Only one rung per ladder was sampled (4+ ER, 3+ BB, 6+ H). Official-scoring conventions (earned versus unearned runs, inherited runners charged to the starter, intentional walks counted, hit versus error) are presumed scoring convention, not Kalshi text. Postponement, scorer changes and the data source are not stated.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box-score statistics (earned runs, hits, walks allowed) for the starter from MLB Stats API or Retrosheet; presumed, since none of the three sampled texts names a source or a post-game scoring-change policy.
variants_and_edge_cases: Earned vs unearned: a run scored after an error or passed ball that would have ended the inning is unearned and does not count; the scorer reconstructs the inning without the error, so a team's error and passed-ball rate is a direct driver of how many runs count for ER rungs.
Inherited runners: runs charged to the starter after he is removed (runners he left on base) count for him, making bullpen quality a driver of his earned runs after exit.
Hits and errors boundary is an official scorer decision and can be changed after the game; walks count intentional walks, not hit-by-pitch.

Starter gate is one batter faced in the sampled KXMLBERA, KXMLBWA and KXMLBHA text. A starter who throws pitches but leaves before facing a batter is undefined by the text (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS, see erhw_zero_batter_starter), so claims that an opener or immediate injury 'settles on tiny counts' are presumptions.
Earned-run, inherited-runner, intentional-walk and hit/error conventions are the official scorer's rules and are assumed here, not stated in the Kalshi text.

hitter_hits_and_total_bases.label: Hitter hits, total bases and hits+runs+RBIs thresholds
hitter_hits_and_total_bases.target: Whether a hitter records at least k hits, total bases or H+R+RBI in the game, requiring appearance per the wording.
hitter_hits_and_total_bases.mechanism: Hits and total bases are sums over plate appearances of per-PA outcome probabilities (single, double, triple, HR vs out), so the expected value is expected PAs (lineup slot, team scoring, substitution risk) times per-PA rates and the distribution is a compound binomial/multinomial. Per-PA rates combine the hitter's contact quality, K and BB, platoon, pitch-type matchup against the starter, park and weather, defence, and later the bullpen; BABIP luck regresses. H+R+RBI adds team-dependent components (runners ahead, hitters behind), increasing variance and correlation with team scoring.

inputs.why: Lineup slot and game script set plate appearances; pinch-hitting and blowout substitution cut them.
Confirmed slot and participation define PAs.
True-talent per-PA outcome rates with projections.
xBA/xSLG and barrel% predict hits/TB beyond results.
Handedness split against starter and bullpen.
Hitter's pitch-type performance against the starter's arsenal.
Starter quality affects first two or three PAs.
Starter's contact suppression and defence behind him.
Relief quality for late PAs: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Park hit and TB factors by handedness.
Weather influences extra-base hit rates.
Speed influences infield hits and extra bases.
Regress BABIP luck: batting average on balls in play deviates from what contact quality and defence imply, and the deviation mostly reverts.
Small, shrunk correction for role/injury changes.
Compound distribution for threshold probabilities.
RBI component of H+R+RBI needs runners ahead.
Runs component needs on-base skill and hitters behind.
Appearance requirement and voids.
Hits and TB rungs for one hitter are nested and linked.
A 3+ hit rung needs a third and often fourth PA, so the truncation survival to PA4 is a first-order determinant.
Total bases and hits for left-handed hitters against righty starters depend materially on the likelihood of facing a left-handed reliever later.
Distinguishes a singles hitter from a power hitter with the same xBA, which matters for the 2+/3+/4+ total-bases rungs.

interactions.hypothesis: PA count x per-PA probability: expected hits = expected PA x P(hit per PA); the lineup slot and team total shift PA while contact quality shifts probability, so both must be in one compound model.
Platoon x pitch-type matchup: same-handed breaking-ball-heavy starters suppress hitters with weak breaking-ball performance, so platoon and pitch-mix effects interact rather than add.
Contact quality x defence/park: expected TB depends on how hard and where a hitter hits the ball relative to park dimensions and fielders, so xSLG should be park- and defence-adjusted.
BABIP luck x recent form: recent hot hitting driven by BABIP should not move the projection, so recent form should enter through contact quality, not batting average.

A 3+ hit rung needs at least three PAs and realistically four, so its probability is a step-like function of the PA distribution: replacing the fifth PA with a pinch hitter moves P(3+ hits) little while losing the fourth moves it a lot. The PA distribution, not the mean, interacts with per-PA hit probability. Stated on the PA-count survival vector crossed with the per-PA hit/total-base probability from the batted-ball outcome model.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare rung calibration using the PA survival vector versus a mean-PA binomial across lineup slots.

interactions.hypothesis: Platoon advantage flips between the starter and later relievers, so the batter's per-PA probability is conditional on pitcher hand by PA index; a lefty hitter vs a righty starter may face two lefty relievers late, offsetting the early advantage. Pitch-type specifics add little on top of hand.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit per-PA hit logit with interaction hand-match x PA index; check sign reversal at PA4-5.

interactions.hypothesis: Total bases depend on the product of contact quality, park gap/wall geometry and runner speed on doubles and triples; a hard-hit line drive in a deep-gap park by a fast runner is worth more than the same ball elsewhere. Park factors for doubles/triples must be applied to the hitter's spray profile, not league-average park multipliers.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare TB prediction with spray-specific park factors versus park-level multipliers.

interactions.hypothesis: In blowouts regulars on the leading team are removed early (PA lost) while on the trailing team they bat to the end; the game-script regime therefore changes both team strength and the hitter's PA, in opposite directions across the two teams.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact team score-state regime with PA survival; test PA4 survival for favorites versus underdogs controlling for slot.

interactions.hypothesis: H+R+RBI counts the same events multiple times, so the components are positively correlated through team scoring and inning clustering; the sum's variance is greater than the sum of component variances. A hitter's own hit adds to all three when he scores and drives himself in.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate the combo through base-out states and compare variance and tail with an independent-sum model.

nonlinearities.shape: Step-like: probability of 3+ hits changes steeply between 3 and 4 PA and little above 5
nonlinearities.why: Hit counts are bounded by PA and rungs at 2+/3+ sit at the boundary of the PA support, so mean-PA linear terms are misleading.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in barrel rate for total bases: each point of barrel% adds more TB than a point of hard-hit or xBA
nonlinearities.why: Total bases weight home runs (4) and extra-base hits (2-3) heavily, so power metrics enter convexly relative to hits.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating regression to expectation; extreme deviations regress further in one-start horizons
nonlinearities.why: BABIP luck is bounded and reverts at a rate depending on balls in play, so one extra hot week should have little weight.

nonlinearities.shape: Piecewise by hit type: doubles and triples respond to gap geometry nonlinearly, HR to carry
nonlinearities.why: Park effects are not uniform across hit types, so a single multiplier distorts TB more than hits.

mechanism_review.summary: A hitter's hits, total bases or hits-plus-runs-plus-RBI are sums over his plate appearances of an outcome that has a multinomial structure: out, walk, single, double, triple, home run. The mean is therefore the number of plate appearances times the per-PA outcome probabilities and the variance is compound. Plate appearances come from lineup slot, the game's total run environment, extra innings and the chance the hitter is removed early (pinch hitter, defensive replacement, blowout rest). Per-PA outcome probabilities come from contact quality and handedness-specific skill met by the starter's arsenal for the first two or three PAs and by relievers (often of the opposite hand, chosen by the manager) for later ones, adjusted for park, weather, defense and BABIP luck. Total bases require the outcome split between singles and extra-base hits; H+R+RBI adds team-driven components of runners on base and hitters behind, making the outcome depend on the whole inning-level scoring process. The contract settles non-starters and zero-PA starters at an undefined fair market price, so the priced distribution is conditional on batting at least once.

stages.name: Lineup gate and slot
stages.description: The market settles anyone not starting or with no PA at the fair market price, so what matters is the confirmed batting order and slot after the card posts: a rest day, platoon sit or late scratch removes the market's population, while the actual slot (leadoff versus eighth) determines the PA budget. Handedness of the opposing starter drives platoon sits for part-time players and the lineup is typically posted a few hours before first pitch.
stages.distribution: Binary start/no-start with timestamped resolution; slot is categorical 1-9 with known PA means (about 4.6 for leadoff down to about 3.7 for ninth).

stages.name: Plate-appearance budget
stages.description: Expected PA equals the batting-order position times the number of times the order turns over, which depends on team run scoring (more runs, more PAs), game length (extra innings, home team not batting in a won ninth) and the chance the starter is removed early. Blowouts and late-game replacements truncate the fifth PA, and PA count is a small discrete variable (3, 4, 5, rarely 6) so thresholds like 3+ hits interact with the PA mass.
stages.distribution: Discrete 3-6 with mass at 4 and 5; correlated with team total; early-removal tail.

stages.name: Per-PA outcome distribution
stages.description: Given a PA, the probabilities of out, walk, single, double, triple and home run come from the hitter's contact quality and plate skill, shifted by pitcher quality and arsenal (platoon, pitch-type), park dimensions and surface, weather and defense (alignment and range). Total bases weights outcomes 1-4, so the extra-base split (power) matters for TB rungs beyond hit probability. BABIP luck regresses toward an expectation set by contact quality and speed.
stages.distribution: Multinomial per PA; hit probability about 0.22-0.30 per PA; TB per PA right-skewed with HR tail.

stages.name: Starter-to-bullpen handoff
stages.description: The first two to three PAs are against the starter; later ones are against relievers whose handedness and quality differ and who are used to create platoon advantages, so a lefty hitter who gets a right-hander starter will often face a lefty reliever late. Which relievers appear depends on the starter's exit time and bullpen availability, and managers pinch-hit for starters in leverage spots which cuts PA.
stages.distribution: Mixture over exit times; reliever handedness is a categorical draw with manager-driven probability.

stages.name: Overlap and count distribution
stages.description: The H+R+RBI ladder is a weighted sum of events that overlap (a home run scores the hitter, counts as a hit and drives in at least one run), and the hits and TB ladders are the same PA sequence aggregated differently. A PA simulation with base-out states gives the joint distribution; per-rung nestedness holds within each ladder.
stages.distribution: Compound multinomial; overdispersed relative to binomial because of shared game environment; H+R+RBI has heavier tail from inning-level clustering.

talent_strength.note: Contact and power talent.

opponent_matchup.note: Starter and reliever matchup.

environment.note: Park and weather by hit type.

pace_volume.note: PA count.

efficiency_conversion.note: BIP to outcome.

distribution_variance.note: Count distribution is derived from the PA-count survival vector and per-PA outcome probabilities, plus the H+R+RBI joint overlap; contact_dist is a target and is not claimed.

settlement_contract.note: Start and one PA gate.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and clinched-seed effects act through the lineup card (who sits) and playing_time_role rather than altering per-PA hit probability, so no separate schedule driver is needed beyond the lineup stage; no motivation effect on a given batter's hit rate is documented.

officiating_rules.note: The settled count is the official scorer's: a borderline hit-versus-error call adds or removes a hit and its total bases, so the park scorer's hit/error tendency is a direct settlement input; the umpire zone effect on hits per PA is small and is not modelled separately.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Yes if the named batter, who must be in the official starting lineup and record at least one plate appearance, finishes the listed game with at least N hits (KXMLBHIT), N total bases (KXMLBTB, singles=1 to home runs=4) or N hits plus runs plus RBIs (KXMLBHRR). A scratch, a bench start, or a starter with no plate appearance pays the fair market price; a player who enters later as a pinch hitter or substitute also settles at the fair market price, and pinch-hit at-bats do not count. So the priced population is 'starts and bats at least once'. Postponement, suspension and rain-shortened handling are not stated in the sampled text; the source of truth is presumably the official box score.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official MLB box score (hits, total bases, runs, RBIs) for the player; presumed MLB Stats API; sampled rules do not name the source.
variants_and_edge_cases: Hits, total bases and hits+runs+RBIs are three ladders on one set of plate-appearance outcomes; a home run adds 1 hit, 4 total bases and at least 3 H+R+RBI points (hit, run, RBI) so the ladders are overlapping, not independent.

Extra innings add plate appearances and, with the automatic runner, runs and RBI chances; a hitter whose PA count differs from the slot expectation because the game goes long is a settlement-relevant tail.

Population is conditional on start and at least one PA; because a late scratch settles at the undefined fair market price rather than on the count, the model can condition on the confirmed lineup but price risk is the in-game removal that reduces PA without voiding.
The hits-allowed, All-Star Game hits and Derby longest-HR series once filed here were moved by the reconciliation; all three remaining series use the batter start-plus-one-PA gate.

hitter_home_runs.label: Hitter home runs (1+ / 2+)
hitter_home_runs.target: Whether a hitter hits at least one (or two) home runs in the game, requiring appearance per the wording.
hitter_home_runs.mechanism: HR per game = 1 - product over PAs of (1 - p_HR), where per-PA HR probability multiplies the hitter's fly-ball/pull/barrel profile by the pitcher's HR vulnerability (by handedness and pitch type), the park's handedness-specific HR factor and the weather (wind component, temperature/air density). Because the base probability is low, multiplicative environment shifts matter and the dominant uncertainty is Bernoulli luck; HR/FB regresses to a contact-quality-determined mean. PA count (batting slot) and the bullpen's HR vulnerability also matter.

inputs.why: Barrel%, pull-air%, FB% and max EV predict HR beyond past HR totals.
Bat speed/squared-up rate adds a stabilising early power signal.
Barrel and hard-hit rates supplement the HR profile.
Pitcher's HR/FB, barrels and fly-ball rate allowed by hand.
Park HR factor by handedness and ball carry environment.
Wind out/in component along the hitter's pull side.
Temperature/humidity/altitude change carry.
Handedness matchup influences HR rate.
Fastball-hitter vs fastball-heavy pitcher matchup.
PA multiplier by slot and team total.
Confirmed lineup and slot: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Later PAs face relievers with different HR vulnerability.
Regress hot/cold HR/FB luck: home runs per fly ball regress strongly to a mean determined by park and contact quality, so past HR luck is not persistent.
1+ and 2+ HR rungs are nested and linked to total HR environment.
Appearance requirement and settlement for postponed/shortened games.
Per-PA home-run probability, compounded over expected PAs, gives the any-HR probability; park, wind and pitcher enter per PA.
Barrel-driven hitters have heavier tails than a constant per-PA rate implies.
Connects hitter spray profile to day-specific carry, a more exact form of the park-by-wind interaction than separate factors.
Team bullpen_talent (xFIP) conflates K/BB with HR; the HR-specific relief exposure is what matters here.
Series HR contracts are priced on exposure, not just per-game HR rate.
Calibrates the 2+ HR rung and joint HR outcomes consistently.
Gives the live KXMLBWALKOFFS contract an explicit exposure-times-rate input; without it the series has no required inputs at all.

interactions.hypothesis: Hitter pull-air profile x park pull-side HR factor x wind: HR probability depends on the hitter's spray direction relative to the park's short side and the wind along that line, so the three should be modelled jointly.
Barrel rate x pitcher HR vulnerability x pitch type: HR risk is highest when a hitter's strong pitch type meets a pitcher who throws it in the damage zone, so matchup is by pitch type and zone.
Air density x wind x park: warm, thin air plus out-blowing wind in a short-porch park compound, but are already partially included in park factors, so use deviation from park norms.
PA count x per-PA HR rate: because per-PA HR probability is small, extra PA from batting slot or team scoring matters almost linearly, interacting with lineup posting and substitution risk.

A pull-power hitter's HR probability is the product of his pull-air barrel rate, the park's wall geometry on that side and the wind component along that line; each alone is mild but together they move per-PA probability by factors of two. The spray direction links the hitter profile to the specific wind and wall, so they must be modelled jointly.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(HR) per batted ball with a spray x wind x park term and compare with a model using separate park and wind factors.

interactions.hypothesis: Per-PA HR probability changes mid-game as the starter is replaced: PAs 1-3 use the starter's vulnerability, PAs 4-5 the reliever's. A homer-prone starter who is pulled early shifts exposure to a different arm, so total HR expectation is a PA-weighted mix conditioned on exit time.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute expected HR with PA-index-specific pitcher vulnerability versus a single starter rate; compare calibration.

interactions.hypothesis: Carry gains from thin air and tailwind add to the park norm but saturate near the wall: a ball that clears by feet gains nothing from more carry while a ball at the warning track gains most. The joint effect is therefore concave in the sum of wind and density and strongest for borderline fly balls.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit P(HR) as logistic in distance-over-wall with wind/density shifting the distance; check concavity in wind and density deviations.

interactions.hypothesis: HRs of hitters in the same game share weather and pitcher-day factors, so P(2+) and any multi-hitter outcome has positive dependence; the 2+ rung for one hitter is sensitive to the shared factor and to his PA count in the extra-inning tail.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed rate of 2+ HR games by hitter strength decile against Poisson-binomial and negative-binomial predictions.

interactions.hypothesis: The 2+ rung needs two home runs, so it is convex in the number of plate appearances: a leadoff hitter in a game with high projected team runs who stays in for a fifth PA has a disproportionately higher P(2+) than a bottom-order hitter at risk of being pinch-hit for late, while P(1+) moves almost linearly. Power hitters are rarely pinch-hit for, so the truncation risk concentrates in platoon and defensive players.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare realised 2+ rates against a linear-in-PA model across lineup slots and game totals, split by pinch-hit-for frequency.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in barrel rate: HR probability per PA rises faster than linearly with barrel% and pull-air%
nonlinearities.why: HRs concentrate in the top tail of exit velocity and launch angle, so power metrics enter convexly; linear barrel terms underprice elite hitters.

nonlinearities.shape: Asymmetric saturating in wind component: gains from tailwind exceed losses from headwind and both saturate at high speed
nonlinearities.why: Carry depends nonlinearly on speed and wall distance; the same wind has different value for borderline versus deep fly balls.

nonlinearities.shape: Near-linear in PA at small p but with a discrete floor/ceiling at 3 and 6 PA
nonlinearities.why: Per-PA probability is small so 1 - (1-p)^PA is almost linear, but discrete support of PA and extra-inning cases create tails.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating shrinkage with fly-ball count: regression weight falls as ln(FB) rises
nonlinearities.why: HR/FB signal stabilises slowly (hundreds of FBs), so early-season HR/FB should be heavily shrunk and later weights grow slowly.

mechanism_review.summary: A home run in a game is the union over the hitter's plate appearances of a low-probability event (about 3 to 6 percent per PA), so P(1+) is approximately 1 minus the product of (1 minus p) over his PAs and P(2+) comes from the tail of a Poisson-binomial. The per-PA probability is a product of hitter power (barrel, pull-air and bat-speed profile), pitcher vulnerability by handedness and pitch type, and a park-weather carry factor that depends on wall geometry in the hitter's spray direction, wind component along that direction, temperature, humidity, altitude and the ball. The number of PAs depends on slot and removal risk, and later PAs face relievers. The event is dominated by Bernoulli luck, so the edge is in the multiplicative environment and matchup terms and in knowing the starter, because HR/FB regresses. Series, window and playoff-count home-run markets are filed in the counting-specials archetype and are not generated here.

stages.name: Participation and PA count
stages.description: The market settles non-starters and zero-PA starters at the fair market price, so the priced population is starters with at least one PA, and the lineup slot plus game length fix the number of HR opportunities. Because per-PA probability is small, expected HRs are almost linear in PA, so lineup posting and early replacement matter proportionally.
stages.distribution: Binary participation resolved at card time; PA count discrete 3-6.

stages.name: Hitter power profile
stages.description: Per-PA HR probability starts with the batter's batted-ball quality (barrels, exit velocity, launch angle), his pull-air rate (home runs are disproportionately pulled fly balls), bat speed and squared-up rate as early signals, and his HR/FB which regresses toward barrel-implied rate. The profile is hand-specific against pitcher handedness.
stages.distribution: Heavy-tailed hitter heterogeneity: per-PA rates from under 1.5% to over 8% across regular hitters.

stages.name: Pitcher and pitch-type vulnerability
stages.description: The starter's HR/FB, barrels allowed, fly-ball rate and the pitch types he throws in hittable locations determine how much of the hitter's power profile is realised; relievers have different HR vulnerability and handedness. The hitter's pitch-type strengths meet the pitcher's usage in damage zones.
stages.distribution: Pitcher HR vulnerability ranges about 0.6 to 1.8 HR/9; relief HR rates differ and are lower sample.

stages.name: Park, wind and carry
stages.description: The same batted ball is a home run in some parks and a fly out in others: wall distance and height by sector, roof state, wind component along the ball's flight path, air density (temperature, humidity, altitude) and ball characteristics determine carry. Because park factors are averages, deviations by hitter spray profile and day-specific wind matter, and the effect is multiplicative on per-PA probability.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative shift from about 0.6 to 1.6 of the neutral per-PA probability; wind adds game-specific variance.

stages.name: Single-game aggregation and within-game dependence
stages.description: Single-game P(1+) and P(2+) come from the Poisson-binomial over the hitter's plate appearances against the starter and then relievers, with the game-shared environment (wind, ball carry, the opposing pitcher's day) adding positive correlation across his PAs. The 2+ rung is far more sensitive to that shared component than the 1+ rung because it needs two events on the same day, and to the chance of a fifth PA in a high-scoring or extra-inning game.
stages.distribution: Poisson-binomial over 3-6 PAs with overdispersion from a game-level random effect; P(2+) roughly proportional to the square of the per-PA rate times a dispersion inflation.

contract_review.settlement_definition: One live series, KXMLBHR (single game; only the 1+ rung was sampled, higher rungs presumed), with sampled rules: Yes if the named batter, who must be in the official starting lineup and record at least one plate appearance, records at least N home runs in the game 'originally scheduled for' the listed date; a scratch or a bench start, a starter with no plate appearance, and a player who enters later all settle at the undefined fair market price, and pinch-hit at-bats do not count. The text is silent on whether extra-inning home runs count (presumed yes, as the official box score includes them), on postponement or suspension of the originally scheduled game, and on a rain-shortened game; no source of truth is named. The playoff-series home-run ladder (KXMLBSERIESHR) moved to the counting-specials archetype.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official MLB box-score home runs for the player (presumed MLB Stats API); the sampled text names no source.
variants_and_edge_cases: Strike construction: 1+ and 2+ rungs on one game are nested events of the same count, so P(2+) <= P(1+) and both come from one per-game HR distribution.

Extra innings, inside-the-park home runs and postponement are not addressed in the KXMLBHR text; the official scorer's count presumably includes extra-inning and inside-the-park home runs (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS, hr_extras_postponement).

Population is conditional on start and at least one PA (rule text), so the priced distribution excludes zero-PA games; the fair-market-price branch replaces what would otherwise be a No for late scratches.

Series totals, playoff league totals, walk-off counts and window markets (KXMLBSERIESHR, KXMLBPLAYOFFHRS, KXMLBWALKOFFS, KXMLBNEXTHR) are filed in the counting-specials archetype and are not modelled here.

hitter_rbis_runs_sb.label: Hitter RBIs, runs scored and stolen bases
hitter_rbis_runs_sb.target: Whether a hitter records at least k RBIs or stolen bases in the game (runs and combos via H+R+RBI are in the hits archetype), requiring appearance per the wording.
hitter_rbis_runs_sb.mechanism: RBI depend on the number of runners on base when the hitter bats (OBP of hitters ahead, team scoring) and the hitter's ability to drive them in (power, contact, situational), so they are heavily context-dependent and high-variance, with lineup slot and team total dominating. Stolen bases require reaching base, deciding to attempt (runner speed, manager, game state) and succeeding against the pitcher's hold time and the catcher's arm, a low-frequency event with rule-regime shifts (pickoff limits, bigger bases). Both markets depend on lineup confirmation and on the opposing starter and catcher.

inputs.why: OBP of preceding hitters and team run environment set RBI chances.
Slot, teammates on base and score state set the opportunity count.
Confirmed slot and surrounding hitters.
Power and contact skill converts runners into RBIs.
Team offence against the starter's hand sets baserunner volume.
Starter quality determines baserunners and run scoring.
Relievers for later PAs: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Steal attempt context: pitcher hold time, catcher pop time.
Runner attempt and success rates.
Sprint speed drives attempts and success.
Rule changes shifted SB attempt and success baselines.
Manager aggressiveness and platoon/pinch-hit style.
Runs depend on on-base skill and hitters behind.
Count distribution for RBI thresholds.
Appearance requirement and SB/CS scoring definitions.
Rungs for the same player share latent opportunity.
Exact RBI-opportunity input for the lineup and opponent; avoids averaging slot opportunity over lineups.
Separates opportunity from conversion so the model knows why a hitter has RBIs; avoids regressing noisy RISP batting average.
Provides an exact per-game decomposition for the 1+ steals ladder instead of season SB rate times PA.
Gives the batting-behind effect on RBI opportunity and stolen-base decisions a measured input instead of leaving it only in an interaction.

interactions.hypothesis: RBI opportunity x power: RBI = (runners on base when batting) x (conversion given hitter), so on-base skill of preceding batters should multiply the hitter's extra-base and contact skill rather than add.

SB attempt: runner speed x pitcher hold time x catcher arm x game state; each factor changes both attempt and success and they must be combined (a slow pitcher with a weak catcher invites attempts by fast runners).
Reaching base x attempt: P(SB) requires the runner to reach first or second, so OBP and expected PA interact with attempt rate, making lineup slot critical.
Rule regime x manager style: the post-2023 rules raised attempts, but managers differ in green-light rates, so regime baselines should be interacted with team style.

RBIs are runners on base times conversion given runners, so a hitter with elite conversion but poor lineup context and a hitter with ordinary conversion in an on-base-heavy lineup can have similar expected RBIs. The product, not a sum, is the right structure, and zero-runner PAs contribute no RBI except a solo home run.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare a model with opportunity x conversion terms versus additive terms on RBI count calibration.

interactions.hypothesis: Steal probability is opportunity times attempt hazard times success; slow pitchers and weak-armed catchers raise both attempt and success for fast runners but have little effect on slow runners, so the battery effect scales with runner speed and manager green light.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit attempt hazard with speed x battery interaction; check coefficient on the interaction.

interactions.hypothesis: The post-2023 rules (bigger bases, pickoff limits) switched league SB attempt and success levels, and teams differ in how much their managers adapted; a model must reset the baseline at the regime boundary and let manager style scale it.
interactions.how_to_test: Train only on 2023+ data and compare with pooled data; include manager x regime term.

interactions.hypothesis: The batter behind a runner affects both RBI opportunity and the steal decision: a strong hitter behind a speedster makes managers less likely to send him early, while a weak batter behind raises steal probability. The lineup order therefore conditions both ladders in opposite ways.
interactions.how_to_test: Add next-batter quality term to steal attempt hazard and RBI opportunity; test sign.

interactions.hypothesis: P(2+ RBI) is convex in the game run environment, which here is carried by the team run-scoring opportunity (rbi_opportunity) shifted by park and opposing starter: low-total games almost never produce 2+ while high-total games do so disproportionately. It is convexity, not a threshold, and uses no market total.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute P(2+ RBI) by decile of team run expectation and compare with predictions from a linear opportunity model.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in team scoring: 2+ RBI probability rises faster than expected runners on base
nonlinearities.why: Multiple RBIs require clustered scoring events (HR with runners, two-run hits), so the right tail grows convexly with run environment.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold (approximate, to be fitted): attempt hazard rises sharply above a sprint-speed cutoff, which the author placed near 28 ft/s, and saturates near elite
nonlinearities.why: Stolen-base attempts concentrate among the fastest runners; the response to speed is flat below a threshold and steep above. The 28 ft/s cutoff is an assumption to be estimated from sprint-speed vs attempt-rate data, not an established fact.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in combined hold time and pop time; the combined-time cutoff (author guess about 3.3 s) is an assumption to be estimated
nonlinearities.why: Steal success is a race against a combined delivery-plus-throw time, which has a sharp advantage zone. The 3.3 s figure is unsourced and depends on time-to-plate data that is not confirmed available.

nonlinearities.shape: Step: moving from slot 3 to slot 5 changes RBI opportunity more than PA because runner volume dominates
nonlinearities.why: PA differences by slot are small, but runner volume per PA rises sharply in the heart of the order, so the effect is nonlinear in slot.

mechanism_review.summary: RBIs and stolen bases are both opportunity-conditional counts. An RBI requires runners on base when the hitter bats and an outcome that brings them home under official scoring, so the expected RBIs are a sum over his PAs of the probability of each base-out state times the probability his outcome scores each runner. The base-out state distribution is determined by the hitters ahead (their on-base rates), team scoring and the opposing pitcher, so it is a Markov chain over the lineup. Conversion depends on power, contact and situational outcomes (sacrifice flies, ground balls scoring from third) and excludes double plays. Stolen bases require reaching first (or second), a steal opportunity with the next base open, a decision to go made by runner, manager and game state, and success against the pitcher's time to plate and the catcher's throw. Both outcomes are rare-event counts with zero mass, heavily dependent on lineup slot and the confirmed lineup, and the count distribution is zero-inflated and overdispersed.

stages.name: Lineup gate and neighbours
stages.description: The market settles non-starters at the fair market price; what matters for the surviving population is the batting slot, who bats ahead (supplying runners) and behind (affecting whether pitchers pitch around him and the stolen-base decision). The lineup card posts late, so ahead-of-him on-base skill is not known until then.
stages.distribution: Binary start gate; neighbour identities change the opportunity distribution materially (a leadoff hitter with a .380 OBP ahead versus a .300 OBP).

stages.name: Runner-on-base opportunity chain
stages.description: Opportunity is the distribution of runners on base when the hitter comes to bat in each of his PAs. It is a Markov chain on the order: the on-base rate of preceding batters, the opposing pitcher's baserunner allowance, and the park run environment determine how often a runner stands on first, second or third (and how many outs), and so how often an RBI is possible at all.
stages.distribution: Discrete base-out state distribution per PA; positive dependence among hitters' states within a game; 40-50% of PAs have no runner on base.

stages.name: RBI conversion given runners
stages.description: Conversion depends on the hitter: power and extra-base rate drive scoring multiple runners, contact and ability to hit fly balls with a runner on third (sacrifice flies), ground-ball tendencies (double plays do not give RBIs) and walk behaviour with the bases loaded. Conversion differs by runner position: a runner on third scores on many outs, a runner on first on few.
stages.distribution: Per-opportunity Bernoulli-like with heavy tail from HR with traffic; correlated with team scoring.

stages.name: Stolen-base attempt and success
stages.description: Stealing needs the hitter on first (or second) with the next base open, then an attempt decision: runner speed and success history, the pitcher's time to the plate and left-handed pickoff, the catcher's pop time and arm, score margin and inning, the manager's green light, and rule changes (bigger bases, pickoff limits) that moved attempt rates. Success then depends on the same battery.
stages.distribution: Rare Bernoulli per opportunity (attempt about 5-10% of first-base opportunities for typical runners, higher for elite); multiple SBs per game possible but rare.

stages.name: Count distribution and ladder nesting
stages.description: RBI and SB counts are zero-inflated and overdispersed relative to a simple Poisson because opportunities cluster in high-scoring innings and one event (a grand slam) can add four; the thresholds 1+ and 2+ for RBI and 1+ for SB are nested events from the same latent opportunity.
stages.distribution: Zero-inflated, right-skewed; RBI heavy tail with clustered runs; SB nearly Bernoulli with small multiple mass.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Two live series with sampled rules: KXMLBRBI (Yes if the named batter records at least N RBIs, e.g. 2+) and KXMLBSB (Yes if he records at least N stolen bases, 1+ sampled). Both use the same gate: the batter must be in the official starting lineup and record at least one plate appearance; a scratch, bench start, zero-PA starter or later-entering substitute settles at the undefined fair market price, and pinch-hit at-bats do not count. The texts say only 'based on RBIs recorded' / 'based on stolen bases recorded'; official-scoring conventions (no RBI on a GIDP, RBI on bases-loaded walk/HBP, no SB on defensive indifference) are presumed. Runs scored have no series. Postponement and the data source are not stated.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box score RBIs from MLB Stats API or Retrosheet; presumed since the sampled rules do not name a source.
variants_and_edge_cases: Two live series are filed here (KXMLBRBI and KXMLBSB); runs scored is not traded, so the 'runs' part of the archetype has no contract evidence. A stolen base credited on a delayed or double steal counts; defensive indifference is scored as no SB by convention (presumed).

Official-scoring ASSUMPTION (the Kalshi text only says 'RBIs recorded'): no RBI on a ground-ball double play; an RBI is credited for a run forced in by a bases-loaded walk, hit-by-pitch or catcher interference/obstruction, and for sacrifice flies; an RBI on an error depends on the scorer's judgement that the run would have scored anyway.

Extra innings: in the regular season the automatic runner on second creates extra RBI chances for the hitters due up in the 10th; the sampled contracts are October postseason games, where MLB does not use the automatic runner, so this effect applies only to regular-season variants.
Postponement and suspended-game handling are not stated in the sampled text.

game_moneyline.label: Game winner, run line and winning margin
game_moneyline.target: Which team wins the game (including extra innings unless worded otherwise), covers a run spread, or wins by a particular margin.
game_moneyline.mechanism: Win probability is built from expected run scoring and prevention for each team at the plate-appearance level: starter quality and expected innings, bullpen quality and availability, confirmed lineup quality against the starter's hand and arsenal, defence, park and weather and the umpire's zone, with a modest home-field effect. The win probability is a function of the run-difference distribution (overdispersed, with extra-innings resolution of ties), so run line and margin contracts need the full distribution rather than the moneyline alone. Late information (confirmed lineups, scratched starters, weather/roof) is the main edge source, and records must be regressed to run-based talent.

inputs.why: Starter quality for each team.
Expected innings determine starter vs bullpen weight.
Confirmed lineup strength vs starter handedness.
Lineup confirmation and rest-day sit-downs.
Availability/fatigue of relievers.
Reliever quality: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Defence and framing: fielders convert balls in play to outs at different rates; catchers add or steal strikes, changing both BABIP and K/BB.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather and wind: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Umpire zone effect: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Late scratches and IL moves: absences change lineup/rotation composition and late scratches can void or reprice player markets.
Travel and schedule: fatigue and travel affect position players' availability, starters' rest and bullpen usage.
Regress luck in team record: team records deviate from run-differential-based expectations because of sequencing, one-run games and bullpen luck, and deviations mean-revert.
Run-difference distribution for spread and margin.
Extra-innings resolution of ties.
Opponent-adjusted team strength.
Sharp-line benchmark: sharp sportsbook and exchange lines are a competing aggregation of information and the standard benchmark for fair probability.
Move after lineup/starter news.
Postponement, suspended game and extras settlement.
The lineup's handedness mix against the starter shifts run expectancy by several percent.
Starter pitch mix against the lineup's pitch-type weaknesses changes strikeout and contact quality.
Confirmed-lineup strikeout rate by handedness is the market-free matchup summary available after lineups post.
Late lineup news is the main non-market source of game-level edge and has no explicit measured input in the catalog beyond a data feed.
Distinguishes between parks with large and small HFA, and handles walk-off truncation correctly for margin strikes.
Distribution tail for run-line and margin contracts, as sketched in the existing run_dist hypothesis but without a measured input.
Fills the regular-season motivation gap for KXMLBGAME-type contracts (late-season starts, rested regulars) that rest_travel and series_context do not address.
KXMLBSTGAME requires a team-strength measure for the players who actually play spring innings and the tie probability the contract does not address.

interactions.hypothesis: Starter innings x bullpen gap: the effective edge from a better starter equals quality gap times expected innings, plus bullpen gap times remaining innings, so workload and bullpen quality should be combined into a weighted pitching rating.

Confirmed lineup x starter handedness x arsenal: lineup strength should be platoon- and pitch-type-specific, so a rested star or lefty-heavy lineup against a righty changes team strength beyond season wRC+.

Run-line cover depends on distribution: favourites win by 2+ less often than win probability suggests because of one-run games and bullpen use when ahead, so margin should come from the run distribution and late-game leverage.
Lineup/starter confirmation timing x price: markets open before lineups, so the edge is how fast the model reprices on confirmation relative to the quote history.

The effective pitching edge is the starter quality gap times the share of innings he covers plus the bullpen gap times the rest, so starter workload acts as a weight that changes with the specific starter and with postseason leashes. A better starter who goes five innings counts for less than the same gap over seven.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute innings-weighted pitching rating versus separate terms; compare win-probability log loss on postseason versus regular season.

interactions.hypothesis: Confirmed-lineup changes matter conditional on the starter's hand and the slot of the missing hitter: a left-handed bat resting against a lefty starter is no loss, while a missing right-handed regular against a lefty is. The same absence has different run value by matchup.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact missing-hitter value with starter hand and slot; test whether the delta is better modelled with hand-specific projections.

interactions.hypothesis: Home advantage concentrates in the late innings: home teams skip the bottom 9th when ahead and win tied games by last bat, so HFA enters margin strikes as truncation and win probability as a tie-resolution bonus, not as a uniform shift in run difference.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate HFA separately for innings 1-8 and 9+ from historical run margins; check effect on spread rungs.

interactions.hypothesis: Large margins are compressed because trailing teams' pitchers are replaced with weaker arms only after the game is out of reach, while narrow leads are protected; the probability of covering a 1.5-run spread is therefore not monotone with a constant-variance model, and fatigued bullpens loosen the compression.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare spread-rung calibration for favorites by bullpen freshness and lead bucket.

interactions.hypothesis: In a postseason single game the series state switches bullpen and starter usage: in elimination games the best relievers pitch more and earlier and starters are pulled at the first sign of trouble, so a starter-quality edge counts for fewer innings and the late-inning margin distribution tightens; in non-elimination games of a lopsided series usage relaxes.
interactions.how_to_test: Backtest series winner probabilities from sequential game models versus constant single-game probability.

interactions.hypothesis: In spring the announced starter's quality matters only for his planned two to four innings, after which depth arms of unknown quality pitch; the effect of a better starter on win probability is therefore cut off at his innings limit, unlike the regular season where an ace's influence extends six or more innings.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress spring game outcomes on starter quality interacted with planned innings and compare the slope with the regular-season slope.

nonlinearities.shape: Logistic-like win probability in expected run difference (about 10% per run near evenly matched), with Pythagorean exponent near 1.8 concave in run ratio
nonlinearities.why: Win probability is a concave-then-saturating function of expected run difference, so large favorites gain progressively less per added run of edge.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating weight: the incremental weight on the starter flattens beyond about 6 innings
nonlinearities.why: The starter's share of innings is bounded and hooks are sharp, so adding workload past six innings adds little to team run prevention.

nonlinearities.shape: Regression coefficient falls with games played; partial pooling toward run-differential talent
nonlinearities.why: The reliability of record versus run-differential grows slowly, so shrinkage weights should depend on sample size nonlinearly.

nonlinearities.shape: Multiplicative scaling of run rate with dispersion scaling (variance rises with park factor)
nonlinearities.why: Hitter-friendly parks raise both the mean and variance of runs, which matters for margin tails.

mechanism_review.summary: The winner and run margin of a baseball game come from two teams' run processes that interact only through the pitchers, the park and the weather. Each team's runs are the sum over innings of base-out Markov outcomes: the starter pitches the first five or six innings against a nine-man lineup, then relievers cover the remainder with leverage-driven deployment. Run expectation per half-inning is determined by the starter's run prevention and workload, the lineup's strength against his handedness and arsenal, the defense and catcher behind him, the park and weather, and the umpire's zone. The difference of two overdispersed, inning-clustered counts, with a tie after nine resolved by an automatic-runner extra-inning game, gives win probability and the whole margin distribution. Moneyline is therefore a single cut of a distribution that spread rungs read in the tail: margin strikes depend on how often relief teams hold or extend leads and on blowout variance. The edge is concentrated in market-moving information that arrives late (confirmed lineup, scratched starter, roof and wind), and records must be regressed to run-based talent. Spring-training games (KXMLBSTGAME) compress team strength because depth players pitch and bat most innings, and they can end tied, which the contract does not address.

stages.name: Who actually pitches and bats
stages.description: Win probability is conditional on the starting pitchers, the nine batters and the catchers who actually play. Probable starters are announced days ahead but change; lineups post a few hours before first pitch and reflect rest days and platoon choices. Before confirmation the market is a mixture over starter and lineup states, so the information structure is a sequence of announcements rather than a single pregame snapshot.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over starter identity (small probability of change) and lineup strength (rest-day sits for regulars cut team strength by a few percent of runs).

stages.name: Team run rates by phase
stages.description: Each team's expected runs are split between the starter's innings and the bullpen's innings. The starter's run prevention (SIERA/xFIP/Stuff+) and expected innings set the weight on starter versus bullpen, the lineup's handedness-specific offence faces the starter's arsenal, and defense and catcher framing adjust balls in play and strikeouts. A better-starter advantage equals the quality gap times expected innings, plus the bullpen gap times the remaining innings.
stages.distribution: Expected runs per team around 3.5-5.5 per game with weighting between starter and bullpen that varies by start (innings ranging from 4 to 7).

stages.name: Environment and officiating
stages.description: Park dimensions and altitude scale run scoring for both teams, with handedness-specific effects; wind and temperature shift carry; the roof can change the day's regime; the umpire's called zone changes walk and strikeout rates for both teams. Home-field advantage is more than constant: last-at-bat advantage and park familiarity matter and vary by park.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative factors on run rates (park factor roughly 0.85 to 1.30); home-field edge a few percentage points of win probability.

stages.name: Run-difference distribution and tie resolution
stages.description: The final margin is a difference of two overdispersed, inning-clustered counts; ties after nine innings go to extra innings: the regular season starts each extra half-inning with an automatic runner on second, but to my knowledge (unverified for 2026) postseason games, which the sampled contracts are, start extras with bases empty, so extras resolve with fewer runs per half-inning and the home team's last-at-bat advantage is the walk-off stopping rule. Margin strikes depend on the skew of this distribution and on bullpen deployment: managers use their best relievers in close games and mop-up arms in blowouts, so winning margins are lumpier than a constant-variance model implies.
stages.distribution: Skellam-like with overdispersion and discrete support; sharp mass at one-run margins; extras resolve ties about even with a home edge.

stages.name: Postseason single-game regime
stages.description: Every sampled contract here is a postseason game, where the state of the series changes the single game: an elimination game pushes managers to use the closer for two innings or a starter on short rest, a team up 3-0 may rest relievers, and travel and off days reset bullpen fatigue. Game win and margin probabilities are therefore conditional on the series state and recent bullpen usage, not only on the listed starters.
stages.distribution: Regime shift in late-inning run prevention (elimination versus non-elimination games); compresses close-game margins and lengthens the one-run tail.

stages.name: Spring-training game regime
stages.description: A spring-training winner depends less on team quality than a regular-season game: starters pitch two to four innings on a ramp-up schedule, regulars leave after a few plate appearances, and the late innings are played by non-roster invitees and minor leaguers whose quality varies widely by club and by split-squad day. Cactus League parks in the Arizona desert inflate scoring relative to Grapefruit League parks, and a game tied after nine may end without a winner, which a literal reading of the winner-only text would settle No for both teams, although no tie clause exists (ml_spring_tie).
stages.distribution: Win probability compressed toward 0.5 (team-strength effect roughly a third of regular season); higher run variance in Arizona parks; a non-trivial tie mass that removes probability from both team markets.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Three live series, all with sampled rules. KXMLBGAME pays Yes if the named team wins the listed game; if the game is postponed or delayed the market stays open and closes after the rescheduled game finishes (within two days), and if it is cancelled or rescheduled more than two days away it resolves to a fair price. KXMLBSTGAME (spring-training winner) uses the same winner and postponement wording ('If Cleveland wins the Cleveland vs Arizona professional baseball game originally scheduled for Mar 24, 2026'), but says nothing about a spring game that ends in a tie, which spring rules allow. KXMLBSPREAD pays Yes if the named team wins by more than the stated run margin (e.g. 5.5) in the game originally scheduled for the date, presumably on the final score including extra innings; the sampled KXMLBSPREAD text has no secondary clause, so its postponement and cancellation handling is unstated rather than inherited from KXMLBGAME. None of the texts addresses a suspended game resumed later or a rain-shortened official game. Division, series and All-Star series formerly filed here were moved by the reconciliation. Source of truth is not named.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official final scores from MLB (Stats API) for winner and margin; the sampled rules do not name the source.
variants_and_edge_cases: KXMLBGAME and KXMLBSTGAME wording covers postponement (open up to two days) and cancellation (fair price) but not a suspended game resumed later or a rain-shortened official game; a postponed game that is replayed within two days usually has different probable starters, so the pre-postponement price refers to a different matchup.

Spread strikes are half-runs, so ties after regulation do not matter for the spread; but extra-inning results do (a 1-run walk-off in the 10th gives margin 1), and the margin is of the completed game's final score.

KXMLBSTGAME (spring training, rules sampled): the text pays only if the named team wins and has no tie clause, while spring games can end tied after nine or after limited extra innings; split squads and mass substitutions mean regulars play only the first few innings, so lineup and pitcher inputs carry over only partially (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS, ml_spring_tie).

Postseason single games (the sampled spread is the Oct 28 2026 Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay game, an interleague pairing and therefore a World Series game) differ from regular-season games: no automatic runner in extras, shorter starter hooks, top relievers on consecutive days and elimination-game usage, so the same matchup implies a different margin distribution.

game_total_and_team_total.label: Game total and team total runs
game_total_and_team_total.target: Whether total runs (or one team's runs) exceed a threshold under the contract's scope (including extra innings, shortened game rules).
game_total_and_team_total.mechanism: Expected runs = sum over plate appearances of per-PA run value for each team, driven by starter quality over the innings he pitches, bullpen run rate for the rest, the lineups' quality by handedness, and multiplicative park/weather/air-density and umpire effects; the realised distribution is overdispersed and inning-clustered so thresholds price tail probabilities. Team totals isolate one offence against the opposing pitching staff and defence. The main edges are late environmental/lineup information (wind, roof, confirmed lineup, scratched starter) and correct dispersion and regression of luck.

inputs.why: Both starters' run prevention.
Starter innings vs bullpen exposure.
Fatigue and availability for the late innings.
Reliever run prevention: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Lineup offence by handedness: a team's lineup quality against the starter's handedness determines runs in the early innings, more than overall season team offence.
Confirmed lineup: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Run factors: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Wind and temperature: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Wind component relative to park axis.
Carry changes: lower air density reduces drag and increases ball carry, raising HR and scoring (Denver, hot days).
Roof open/closed controls weather effect.
Zone effect: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Contact allowed and defence: hits allowed depend on the quality of contact against a pitcher and the fielders converting it into outs.
Fielding and catcher framing: fielders convert balls in play to outs at different rates; catchers add or steal strikes, changing both BABIP and K/BB.
Regress BABIP in team samples.
League run environment: league-wide rule and equipment changes shift league baselines for steals, BABIP, pace and run scoring between seasons.
Overdispersion and tail shape.
Extra innings add runs where counted.
Total and team total rungs consistency.
Counting of extra innings, shortened and suspended games.
Directly changes total thresholds near the median, especially for strong home favorites, and is absent from the existing catalog.

The existing catalog assumes extras count but the sampled rules are silent; the input keeps the dependence explicit and testable. Re-specified by regime because all sampled totals are postseason games, where the automatic runner is not used to my knowledge.
KXMLBSERIESGAMES settles directly on series length; no catalog input models it.

interactions.hypothesis: Wind x air density x park: HR/fly-ball effects are multiplicative in HR-friendly parks, so weather adjustments should be computed from deviations from park norms and interacted with park HR factor and fly-ball tendencies.
Starter exit x bullpen state: totals are a mixture of starter and bullpen run rates by inning, so starter workload and bullpen availability/quality interact to give the late-inning scoring.
Umpire zone x walk-prone pitcher/lineup: a small zone raises totals most when a pitcher is walk-prone and lineups are patient, so umpire effects should depend on plate-discipline matchup.
Dispersion x threshold: high-total and low-total rungs price tails; park and weather affect variance as well as mean (Coors, wind games), so dispersion should depend on environment.

Park factor, wind and air density multiply the same fly-ball carry, so in a hitter's park with a tailwind and thin air the effects compound; deviations from park norms, not absolute weather, carry the information, and the effect is largest for fly-ball-heavy lineups and starters.
interactions.how_to_test: Model run multiplier as park x exp(beta_wind*wind_dev + beta_air*density_dev) and compare with additive terms.

interactions.hypothesis: The total is a mixture of starter-run and bullpen-run innings, so the sensitivity of the total to starter quality depends on how long he goes, which depends on bullpen state and leash. A depleted bullpen lengthens the leash and thereby increases weight on the starter's quality.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact starter quality with exit-time distribution and bullpen freshness; check total residual by those terms.

interactions.hypothesis: A smaller called zone raises walks and run scoring most for patient lineups against command-poor pitchers, and a larger zone helps pitchers with edge-heavy approach; umpire effect scales with the matchup's walk exposure rather than adding a fixed number of runs.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact umpire zone residual with lineup chase rate and pitcher zone rate in a walk model; test total residuals.

interactions.hypothesis: In high-run environments variance rises faster than the mean (clustering of crooked-number innings), so the probability of totals above the model median falls less than a constant-variance model implies, and the under side is more exposed at low thresholds.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate dispersion as a function of park factor and wind-out indicator; compare calibration of thresholds near 10 runs in Coors versus pitcher's parks.

interactions.hypothesis: Game-length regime: when the home team leads, the bottom of the ninth is skipped (negative total adjustment); when tied, extras add runs; when the home team trails, the game runs to completion. The three regimes sit at different parts of the run-difference distribution, so the expected total is a mixture with different slopes.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition historical totals on score state after eight innings and compare to unconditional total model.

nonlinearities.shape: Overdispersed negative-binomial tail: P(total >= 11) is several times a Poisson prediction
nonlinearities.why: Runs cluster in innings and crooked numbers amplify, so the right tail is heavy relative to a Poisson with the same mean; thresholds are priced in the tail.

nonlinearities.shape: Asymmetric saturating: out-blowing wind adds more carry than in-blowing wind removes, both saturate beyond about 15 mph
nonlinearities.why: Carry gains and losses at the wall are not symmetric and flatten at high wind speeds.

nonlinearities.shape: Roughly linear in density for HR carry, convex for hit-by-hit effects at altitude
nonlinearities.why: Reduced drag accumulates over a long flight, so the benefit rises more in the far outfield; Coors differs qualitatively.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex penalty for poor starters: a bad starter's extra runs per inning are larger because bullpen exposure grows and leverage rises
nonlinearities.why: A weak starter exits early, exposing the bullpen and raising run totals more than his rate gap alone suggests.

mechanism_review.summary: Total runs are the sum of two teams' runs, each the sum over innings of a clustered run process. For a team, expected runs equal the opposing starter's run prevention over the innings he covers plus the bullpen's rate over the rest, applied to the lineup's strength against that starter's hand and arsenal, then scaled multiplicatively by park, wind, air density and the umpire's zone, with defense adjusting balls in play. The distribution is overdispersed because runs cluster in big innings that start from baserunners and are amplified by home runs and relievers entering. Totals are therefore not a symmetric band around a mean: thresholds near the median price the shape of the right tail, which depends on environment (Coors, wind blowing out) that changes variance as well as the mean. Structural details matter: the home team's bottom of the ninth is not played when it leads, extra innings add runs (with an automatic runner) if the contract counts them, and a postponed or shortened game changes the sum. Series-length markets left this archetype and are not generated here.

stages.name: Pitching matchup and workload
stages.description: Runs allowed by each pitching staff come first from the listed starter and how long he pitches, then from the relievers who finish. The starter's true-talent run prevention, innings expectation and the manager's leash determine the split, and a scratch of the listed starter changes the total by a large amount. Bullpen availability changes late-inning rates.
stages.distribution: Mixture over starter exit time (4-7 innings) and over bullpen composition; scratch risk as rare regime.

stages.name: Lineup offence and matchup
stages.description: Each team's offence is the confirmed nine facing the specific starter: handedness-specific wRC+, order slot weights, and contact quality versus the starter's profile. Defense and catcher framing shape balls in play and strikeouts on the pitching side.
stages.distribution: Per-team expected runs about 3.5-5.5 with sd of expectation uncertainty about 0.4 runs from lineup and starter information.

stages.name: Run-environment multipliers
stages.description: Park factors, altitude, wind direction relative to the park axis, temperature and humidity (air density), roof state, ball regime and the umpire's called zone scale run scoring multiplicatively; the day-specific deviation from park norms is the information, because the park average is already priced. Variance increases with run environment.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative on mean runs (about 0.85-1.35); heteroskedastic: variance grows with the environment.

stages.name: Run distribution, truncation and extras
stages.description: Realised totals are drawn from an overdispersed, inning-clustered distribution. The home team may not bat in the ninth; a tie after nine brings extra innings, which in the regular season start each half-inning with an automatic runner on second (about one run per half-inning) but in the postseason start with the bases empty (roughly half that), and those runs matter only if the contract counts them. The right tail of the total thresholds (10+ runs) is driven by big innings and weak-bullpen blowups.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed discrete (negative-binomial-like) per team, correlated positively across teams via shared park and weather; truncated by bottom-9 skip and extended by extras.

stages.name: Postseason run-environment regime
stages.description: The sampled totals are from the Oct 28 2026 Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay World Series game (an interleague pairing), where run scoring follows a different regime from the regular season: starters are pulled earlier but replaced by the best relievers rather than long men, cold October weather in northern parks suppresses carry, rotations shorten to the top three or four starters, and extras have no automatic runner. Game and team totals must be priced with postseason-specific starter and bullpen splits rather than regular-season team averages.
stages.distribution: Downward shift of the total's mean and a thinner right tail relative to a regular-season game with the same listed starters; extras contribution roughly halved.
