contract_review.settlement_definition: Two live series with sampled rules: KXMLBTOTAL pays Yes if the two teams collectively score more than the strike (e.g. 8.5 runs, text 'collectively score more 8.5 runs') in the listed game; KXMLBTEAMTOTAL pays Yes if the named team scores N or more runs (title 'over 7.5', rule '8+'). The sampled rules do not state whether extra-inning runs count, whether an unplayed bottom of the ninth changes anything, or how postponed, suspended and rain-shortened games settle. The series-length markets formerly filed here moved to the playoff-series archetype. Source of truth is not named.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official game score (MLB Stats API / box score) for game and team totals; source not named in the sampled rules.
variants_and_edge_cases: Whether extra-inning runs count toward game and team totals is not stated in the sample (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS); the existing catalog assumes they do, but the settlement text is silent.
When the home team leads after 8.5 innings the bottom of the ninth is not played, truncating both the game total and the home team total relative to a nine-inning-per-side expectation.
Team total wording differs between title (over 7.5) and rule (8+): the rule text governs and both describe 8 or more runs.
Postponed or suspended games remain tied to the 'originally scheduled' game, but the sample gives no explicit treatment.

Both sampled totals are October postseason games: MLB's automatic extra-innings runner applies to the regular season only, so postseason extras add runs at roughly the bases-empty late-inning rate and a regular-season total with the same pregame expectation has a fatter extras tail.

first_inning_and_inning_markets.label: First-inning runs and inning-level markets
first_inning_and_inning_markets.target: Whether runs are scored in a specific inning (first inning or other inning), which team outscores the other in the inning, or the inning's run total.
first_inning_and_inning_markets.mechanism: An inning is a short Markov process through base-out states with outcomes depending on the three hitters due up and the pitcher on the mound; for the first inning the top three of each lineup face the fresh starter, so the run probability (YRFI) is the union of two half-innings with probabilities driven by top-order on-base skill, handedness and starter first-trip command. Later-inning markets additionally depend on which batters are due, TTO penalty and bullpen entry, which are partly unknowable pregame. Small samples make historical first-inning splits mostly noise; PA-level simulation is preferred.

inputs.why: First-inning scoring distribution baseline.
The first three batters, not the whole lineup, decide the first inning.
Confirmed top-three hitters and order.
Handedness of top-order hitters vs starter.
Starter quality in the first trip through the order.
Early walks and zone rate: walks arise when pitchers miss the zone and hitters take pitches outside it; both the pitcher's command and the lineup's discipline matter.
K% reduces baserunners: strikeouts occur when a pitcher's swing-and-miss and called-strike ability meet hitters prone to striking out; lineup K% by handedness captures the hitter side.
First-three-innings pattern: the first three innings give every starter a full turn through the top of the order and are mostly pitcher-quality and lineup-top dependent.
Later-inning markets depend on trip through order.
Bullpen entry for later innings.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Temperature and wind: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Early-game zone effect: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Inning-level distribution: runs per team per game are overdispersed and inning-clustered, so threshold and total markets depend on distribution shape and the correlation between teams.
Rules for shortened/postponed games and extra innings in inning markets.
BABIP luck in the starter's recent first innings regresses; raw first-inning ERA overstates persistent skill.
Replaces first_inning_splits as a computational estimand and removes dependence on 30-start samples.
The ninth is a state-conditional, non-exchangeable inning; no existing catalog input captures the skipped-bottom and closer selection.
Provides the base rate by inning index and a ceiling for how much inning-specific tendency is real.

interactions.hypothesis: Top-three OBP x starter command: first-inning scoring requires baserunners from top hitters against the starter's zone and walk rate, so the product by half-inning and the two-half-inning union give the event probability.

Handedness x starter first-trip arsenal: lefty-heavy top order against a righty with a weak changeup changes first-inning run probability beyond aggregate wRC+, so platoon should be applied to the top three.
Small-sample first-inning splits x PA-level simulation: observed first-inning ERA is mostly noise, so it should enter only as a heavily shrunk adjustment to the PA-level model.

A run in the first inning requires baserunners from the top three and then enough extra-base power or walks to convert, so the probability depends on the product of leadoff on-base skill, the number-three hitter's power and the pitcher's walk rate rather than their sum. A lineup top with two high-OBP hitters against a command-poor starter compounds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare RFI log loss from the chain (product) versus additive top-three wOBA models.

interactions.hypothesis: The ninth-inning run distribution has three regimes: save situation with closer (low run probability), tied or one-run with high-leverage arms, and blowout with mop-up arms; home-bats flag changes whether the bottom exists. The regime probabilities come from the score distribution, so ninth-inning markets are a mixture priced by margin.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(run in top-9) by entry margin bucket and closer availability; compare with unconditional average.

interactions.hypothesis: Whether the ninth is played at all, and how many runs it can contain, depends on the margin entering the bottom half: a home lead removes it, a tie or one-run deficit ends it at the go-ahead run, and the due-up hitters set how often that run arrives. The truncation lowers over-1.5 and Tie-strike probabilities relative to the untruncated half-inning run distribution, most for tied games with a high-OBP due-up group.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed bottom-9 run distributions for tied-entering and trailing-entering games against the untruncated Markov chain output, split by due-up OBP tercile.

interactions.hypothesis: Platoon advantage of the top of the order is conditional on the starter's pitch arsenal: a lefty-heavy top against a right-hander with a good changeup differs from the same top against a slider-only right-hander; the effect is realised in the first trip where hitters have not adjusted.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact top-four handedness share with starter changeup/slider usage in a first-trip PA model.

interactions.hypothesis: The KXMLBINNINGWIN tie strike is a joint event of top- and bottom-9th runs: when the home team leads it equals P(visitors score 0 against the home closer or setup man); when tied or trailing the home half is truncated at the winning run, so a 1-1 or 2-2 ninth is rarer than independent half-innings imply and 0-0 dominates. The weight on each case comes from the margin distribution entering the ninth and from which relievers are available.
interactions.how_to_test: Tabulate historical 9th-inning run pairs by entering margin and compare tie frequency with a model that treats the two halves as independent untruncated innings.

nonlinearities.shape: Zero-inflated, convex: P(run) rises convexly with top-three OBP because the chain compounds across hitters
nonlinearities.why: Extra baserunners make each later batter more valuable (runner-on states), so the probability of at least one run grows faster than linearly in on-base skill.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating weight with innings pitched: weight on pitcher-specific first-inning history rises slowly and stays low
nonlinearities.why: First-inning outcomes are rare events with heavy sampling noise; the shrinkage weight should grow roughly with the number of innings but remain small.

nonlinearities.shape: Discrete mass at 0 runs per inning (about 72%) with geometric tail
nonlinearities.why: Inning scores are zero-inflated so a normal approximation fails for 0.5 and 1.5 strikes.

nonlinearities.shape: Step by margin entering the ninth: save situation (lead 1-3) versus blowout
nonlinearities.why: Pitcher quality and run probability change discontinuously around the save-situation boundary.

nonlinearities.shape: Absorbing truncation: the bottom-9 run count is capped at the margin needed to take the lead (plus homer exception)
nonlinearities.why: The home half ends on the go-ahead run, so P(2+ runs in the bottom 9) is far below the untruncated chain value in tied or one-run games; this is a stopping-rule nonlinearity distinct from the save-situation step.

mechanism_review.summary: An inning is a short Markov process over base-out states: batters come up in lineup order, each plate appearance moves the state, and the half-inning ends after three outs, giving a zero-inflated run distribution whose probability of at least one run is about a quarter to a third. For the first inning the three or four hitters due up at the top of each order face the starter's first trip, so the probability of a run in the first inning (RFI) is the union of two half-innings driven by top-of-order on-base and power skill, handedness, and the starter's first-inning command. Later-inning markets depend on which batters are due, the times-through-the-order effect and which reliever enters; the ninth inning is special because the home team may not bat and the pitcher is usually a high-leverage reliever chosen by game state. A first-principles model is a plate-appearance simulation with base-out states and pitcher-specific, count-based outcome probabilities, with strong shrinkage because inning-split samples are tiny. The cumulative F3/F5/F7, extras and winning-streak series were moved to other archetypes and are not generated here.

stages.name: Which hitters and which pitcher are in the inning
stages.description: The first inning is deterministic in who bats first: slots 1-3 of the visiting side against the starter, then 1-3 of the home side, with slot 4 and 5 appearing only if baserunners accumulate. Ninth-inning markets instead depend on the due-up slots at that point and on the pitcher chosen by score state (closer, setup, mop-up), neither known pregame. The identity and handedness of these few players is the dominant information.
stages.distribution: Deterministic for first inning, mixture over due-up slots and reliever identity for later innings.

stages.name: Half-inning base-out Markov process
stages.description: From the bases-empty, zero-out state each PA transitions among states according to the batter-pitcher outcome probabilities (walk, single, double, home run, strikeout, ball in play out); the half-inning ends at three outs. P(at least one run) is the probability of leaving the zero-run absorbing path, and expected runs per inning follow. The top three hitters' OBP and extra-base power set the entry probability and the pitcher's early command sets walks.
stages.distribution: Zero-inflated geometric-like run count per half-inning (P(0) around 0.7 to 0.75), heavier tail when runners accumulate.

stages.name: First-trip pitcher state and zone
stages.description: The starter's first trip through the order combines fresh stuff with command variance; early innings also have an umpire-zone effect and park/weather shifts, but historical first-inning splits for a single pitcher are noisy (about 30 starts per season), so inference needs heavy shrinkage toward the pitcher's PA-level skill rather than first-inning ERA.
stages.distribution: Small-sample noise dominates observed first-inning splits; true variation across pitchers is small relative to sampling error.

stages.name: Game-state conditioning for late innings
stages.description: The ninth inning depends on the score entering it: tied, one-run, save situation, blowout; the home team skips the bottom of the ninth when leading, which zeroes its 9th-inning runs and turns the inning-winner tie strike into 'visitors held scoreless'; pitcher choice follows leverage (closer in save situations, setup arms when tied, mop-up arms in blowouts). The bottom of the ninth is a stopping-rule process: the half-inning ends the moment the home team takes the lead, so the home half's runs are truncated (a walk-off home run counts all its runs; any other walk-off counts only the runs needed to take the lead), which biases a naive over-1.5 or tie estimate.
stages.distribution: State-dependent mixture over entering margin; point mass at 'bottom half not played' (home leading, roughly half of games) and a truncated home half otherwise.

stages.name: Called-game fair-price branch
stages.description: The 9th-inning markets resolve to a Fair Price if the game is called before the 9th is completed, while KXMLBRFI has no such clause and is settled once the first inning is played. A weather-shortened game is therefore a separate settlement branch for late-inning strikes: its probability depends on rain timing relative to the game's progress, and it removes the 9th-inning outcome from the payoff rather than settling it.
stages.distribution: Rare branch (a few percent of outdoor games, near zero under a roof) that grows with forecast precipitation late in the game window; zero for first-inning markets once the first inning completes.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Three live series after the reconciliation, all with sampled rules. KXMLBRFI pays Yes 'If either team scores a run in the first inning' (no secondary clause on postponement or called games). KXMLBINNINGTOTAL (over N runs in the named inning, e.g. over 1.5 in the 9th) and KXMLBINNINGWIN (which team scores more in the named inning, with a tie strike 'If neither ... scores more runs') count 'Only runs scored during the 9th inning', settle 'even if the home team does not bat in the bottom of the inning', and resolve to a Fair Price if the game is called before the inning is completed. Only the 9th-inning strike was sampled. The F3/F5/F7, extras and winning-streak series formerly filed here were moved by the reconciliation. Source of truth is not named.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official linescore by inning (MLB Stats API / box score); presumed, since the sampled rules name no source.
variants_and_edge_cases: Population differs by series: KXMLBRFI resolves on the first inning (both halves always played), while KXMLBINNINGTOTAL and KXMLBINNINGWIN resolve on the named (sampled: 9th) inning, whose bottom half may not be played or may end early on a walk-off.

Ninth-inning markets: the home team does not bat when leading, so the ninth is an at most one-half-inning event in about half of games, and the market still settles Yes/No on the visitor's runs; a game called before the 9th is completed resolves to a Fair Price.

Inning-winner construction: when the home team leads after 8.5 innings it does not bat, its 9th-inning runs are zero, so the tie strike resolves Yes exactly when the visitors are held scoreless in the top of the 9th and the home strike cannot win; when the home team bats, a non-home-run walk-off caps its 9th-inning runs at the margin needed, while a walk-off home run counts every run it scores.

KXMLBRFI has a one-sentence rule ('If either team scores a run in the first inning') with no clause for a postponed, suspended or called game, unlike the 9th-inning markets, which resolve to a Fair Price if the inning is not completed.

first5_markets.label: First-five-innings winner, spread and total
first5_markets.target: First-five-innings result (winner/run spread) or total runs through five innings.
first5_markets.mechanism: Through five innings runs are scored mostly against the starters (typically two trips through the order), so the market is driven by starter quality, expected exit before the fifth, the lineups' strength against the starter's hand, and the environment, with the bullpen entering only after early exits. Relative to full game, bullpen strength is de-emphasised and starter leash risk is emphasised, and ties are possible so spread and winner contracts differ by tie handling.

inputs.why: Starter run prevention for innings 1-5.
Separation of starter vs bullpen run rates.
Probability of exit before the fifth inning.
Third time through the order raises run expectancy materially, so the starter's expected depth sets the first-five mean.
Lineup strength vs starter's hand.
Confirmed lineup: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Handedness composition: same-handed matchups favour pitchers (especially vs breaking balls), opposite-handed matchups favour hitters, and the size of the split differs by player.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Umpire zone for the early innings.
Contact allowed and defence: hits allowed depend on the quality of contact against a pitcher and the fielders converting it into outs.
Overdispersed F5 run distribution and tie probability.
Bullpen relevance in early exit cases.
Tie/push treatment and shortened-game rule for F5 markets.
ERA-minus-FIP gaps from stranding luck regress and mis-price first-five runs.
Without a refund clause the change risk is not hedged; it is a primary driver of early-market error.
Converts the confirmed lineup into five-inning exposure rather than a nine-inning average.
F5 differs from full game in how much bullpen enters; this is the explicit mixture weight.

interactions.hypothesis: Exit before the fifth: F5 run rate is a mixture of starter-only and bullpen-inclusive, so leash and bullpen state interact with starter quality.
Top-of-order exposure x handedness: in five innings the top of the lineup bats twice, so platoon quality of the top six hitters is weighted more than in a full game.
Tie handling x run distribution: F5 ties are common enough that push/loss rules change pricing; the discrete distribution and rule jointly define the probability.

F5 run rate is a mixture of starter-only innings and starter-plus-reliever innings: a good starter with a short leash pushes relievers into the fifth, while a mediocre starter with a long leash keeps them out, so the expected value depends on exit probability times the quality gap between starter and reliever.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit F5 runs on mixture weights from the exit hazard; compare residual by starter exit tercile.

interactions.hypothesis: Because slots 1-4 bat twice within five innings, platoon advantage at the top of the order is weighted more than in a full game; a lefty-heavy top four against a righty starter inflates F5 runs by more than the team-level wRC+ suggests. Tested at slot level as batter handedness (from the confirmed card) crossed with the starter hand, weighted by expected first-five PA, rather than against the duplicate platoon team aggregate.
interactions.how_to_test: Contrast F5 runs for lineups whose slots 1-4 are platoon-advantaged against the starter hand versus those whose slots 5-9 are, holding total team wRC+ vs hand fixed.

interactions.hypothesis: The second-trip penalty arrives at about the 10th batter and is larger for pitchers with narrow arsenals, so the effect is discontinuous in batters faced and has a pitcher-specific size; strand luck regression changes how much of an early-inning performance the model attributes to the starter.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate trip-specific run rates by pitcher arsenal width; test breakpoint at BF 9-10.

interactions.hypothesis: Tie handling and starter-change risk combine: a starter swap shifts the whole score distribution while the Tie strike pays on equal scores, so the joint PMF is a mixture over starter states with tie mass concentrated in low-total states.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute tie probability by mixture state and compare to observed tie rate by listed-starter-changed flag.

interactions.hypothesis: The umpire zone matters most in low-offence environments where each walk is a bigger share of baserunners, and park/weather push toward the same margin; the interaction is a threshold in run environment where zone effects dominate pitcher's parks.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact umpire zone residual with park factor tercile in a five-inning runs model.

interactions.hypothesis: The F7 result depends on how many of innings six and seven each bullpen must cover and which relievers are available: a tired bullpen after an extra-inning game forces lower-leverage arms into the sixth, and a manager leading by a run uses setup men earlier, so the same starters imply different F7 distributions by bullpen state.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare F7 scoring against F5 scoring split by bullpen pitches thrown over the previous three days and by score margin after five.

nonlinearities.shape: Step at the second and third trip boundaries in batters faced
nonlinearities.why: Run-prevention penalties apply at trip boundaries rather than smoothly, so a linear innings term misprices exit-time-weighted runs.

nonlinearities.shape: Heavily discrete with excess mass at 0 and 1 runs per team in five innings
nonlinearities.why: Low-scoring five-inning games have large tie mass; a continuous approximation misprices spread and tie strikes.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex penalty for weak starters because early exits bring in relievers
nonlinearities.why: The effective run rate for a poor starter is worse than his rate suggests because of early exits and inherited-runner effects.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating shrinkage of team-level F5 split to league mean
nonlinearities.why: Team F5-versus-bullpen splits are noisy and mostly random, so the shrink weight should be heavy and nonlinear in sample size.

mechanism_review.summary: Runs in the first five innings are produced almost entirely by the two starters and their lineups, with the bullpen entering only after an early exit. Each starter faces the opposing order roughly twice, so the first five innings weight the top six hitters of each lineup more heavily than a nine-inning game does, and the times-through-the-order penalty applies across the second trip. The expected score per team is therefore the starter's run prevention over an exit-time distribution (an early pull exposes relievers) against the confirmed lineup by handedness, scaled by the park, weather and the umpire's zone, which is more influential early. Because the half-inning run process is clustered and discrete, five-inning margins are lumpy and ties are frequent enough that the winner, spread and total contracts differ materially: the winner market has a Tie strike, the spread a margin, the total a sum. Bullpen strength matters less than in the full game; starter leash and opener usage matter more. The sampled rules do not void a starter change, so late scratches are priced risk.

stages.name: Listed starters and change risk
stages.description: Because the contract is not conditioned on the pitcher, the starter announced earlier might be replaced by another starter or an opener at any time before first pitch, and the market sits on the pre-announcement distribution until the lineup confirms. The distribution over actual starters is the first stage; its variance is large in postseason and when the listed pitcher is on a minor injury.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over starter identity with rare but high-impact switches; resolved at lineup post and first pitch.

stages.name: Starter run prevention across two trips
stages.description: Over the first five innings the starter faces the order about twice, and some starters a third time. Run prevention per trip falls for most pitchers on the second look, with a larger penalty for pitchers with few pitch types, while pitchers who exit before the fifth hand innings to relievers with a different rate. The mix over exit times is the key distribution.
stages.distribution: Mixture over exit time (about 4-6.5 innings); trip-specific run rates with second-trip penalty.

stages.name: Lineup slots weighted by first-five exposure
stages.description: In five innings each team sends about 21-23 batters to the plate, so slots 1-4 bat twice and often slots 5-6 twice if the offence is productive, while slots 7-9 are weighted less. The confirmed order and its handedness against the starter determine the weight on each hitter's skill set, and platoon advantages of the top of the order dominate.
stages.distribution: Slot exposure weights from a Markov chain; top-6 weight roughly 2/3 of PAs.

stages.name: Environment and zone early in the game
stages.description: Park dimensions, altitude, wind, temperature and the roof scale run scoring from the first pitch, and the plate umpire's zone is a large early-game effect because the early innings are pitched by the starters; contact quality and defense (balls in play) shape hits allowed.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative factor on run rate with higher variance in hitter-friendly parks; umpire effect about a few percent of runs.

stages.name: Discrete score distribution and tie mass
stages.description: The five-inning score is a pair of discrete overdispersed counts; the tie probability (about one game in eight) is the sum over equal scores and is sensitive to the total: low-total games tie more. The three contracts read this distribution differently (Tie strike, margin strikes, total strikes), so the model must output the full joint PMF.
stages.distribution: Skellam-like with extra clustering; tie mass concentrated at 0-0, 1-1, 2-2.

stages.name: Three- and seven-inning windows
stages.description: KXMLBF3 settles after three innings, so it is almost entirely the two starters' first trip through the order against the top of each lineup, with first-inning scoring weighting heavily. KXMLBF7 adds innings six and seven, which most starters do not finish: the result depends on each bullpen's quality and availability after recent usage and on managers' leverage choices when leading or trailing late, so the F7 tie mass and margin are shaped by middle relief rather than starters.
stages.distribution: F3: low totals with tie mass near 0.3 (0-0 and 1-1 dominate); F7: cumulative scores close to full-game shape with tie mass around 0.12, mixed over bullpen availability states.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Five live series, all with sampled rules, now filed here: KXMLBF5, KXMLBF3 and KXMLBF7 (winner of the first 5/3/7 innings with a 'Tie' strike: if the score at the end of the named inning is tied the Tie strike resolves Yes and all team strikes No), KXMLBF5SPREAD (named team wins the first five innings by more than a margin, e.g. 2.5) and KXMLBF5TOTAL (combined runs in the first five innings more than a strike, e.g. 6.5). All say a postponed or delayed game keeps the market open and it closes after the rescheduled game finishes (within two days). No pitcher clause appears, so a starter change does not void. A game called before the named inning completes is not addressed. Source of truth is not named.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official linescore at the end of the third, fifth and seventh innings (MLB Stats API / box score) for F3, F5/F5SPREAD/F5TOTAL and F7; not named in the sampled rules.
variants_and_edge_cases: INFERENCE (no pitcher clause appears in the sampled rules, so silence is read as no void): a changed or scratched starter is assumed not to void the F5 market, so starter-change risk is priced rather than refunded, unlike the player-prop ladders. Not confirmed by any explicit rule.
Winner markets have three strikes (each team and Tie); spread and total markets have no tie strike, so a tied score after five matters differently across the three contracts.
A game called before the fifth inning is complete (rain) is not addressed in the sampled text (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS); 'delayed' games stay open for up to two days.
Related strikes exist for 3 and 7 innings (KXMLBF3, KXMLBF7), which shift weight between starter and bullpen.

extras_and_delay.label: Extra innings and game delay/postponement
extras_and_delay.target: Whether the game goes to extra innings (tied after nine) or whether a delay/postponement occurs, per the contract definition.
extras_and_delay.mechanism: Extra innings are the event that the two run totals tie after nine, so probability is a function of the run distribution (higher in low-total, close games) and of late-inning scoring, with the ghost runner shaping what happens after but not the event. Delay markets are weather-timing problems: probability of precipitation or lightning near first pitch relative to roof status and umpire/team decision behaviour, mostly independent of team quality. Both are low-to-moderate probability events decided by distributional shape and exact contract wording (start delay vs in-game delay, suspended-game treatment).

inputs.why: Tied-after-nine rate by total/spread bucket.
Distribution shape drives P(tie).
Strong starters lower scoring and increase tie chance.
Late-inning scoring quality: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Low-scoring environments tie more.
Extra-inning strategy affects length of extras.
Historical delay rates and risk model.
Hourly precipitation and radar nowcast around first pitch.
Closed roof removes weather delay risk.
Lightning, wind and temperature.
Delay, suspension and postponement definitions.
Contract wording for extras and delay windows.
Market close vs actual first pitch time.
KXMLBEXTRAS settles on the tie event, so the joint distribution (not each team's total) is the right object.
Defines P(extras) as P(level score after nine complete innings) so both extras routes are included.
Distinguishes lightning-driven from rain-driven delays and sharpens the weather gate.
Defines the empirical event frequency and tests the sensitivity of the market to the recording threshold.

interactions.hypothesis: Total x spread: tie probability peaks when expected total is low and teams are evenly matched, so total and spread jointly drive extra-innings probability and should come from one run-distribution model.
Precipitation timing x roof state: the same forecast produces a delay only if the roof is open and the rain overlaps the game window, so roof state gates the weather risk.

Delay definition x time window: contracts counting only start delays are driven by pre-first-pitch weather, in-game delay contracts add game-length exposure (including extras), so the definition interacts with extra-innings probability.

Extras probability is the diagonal of the joint score distribution; shared park and weather push both teams' runs the same way, increasing diagonal mass at any given total. The effect is largest in extreme parks where the common factor is largest.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit bivariate NB with park-specific correlation and compare tie frequency by park to independent convolution.

interactions.hypothesis: Delay probability is the product of weather overlapping the window and the roof being open; for retractable roofs the decision to close depends on forecast confidence, so closed-roof parks have near-zero delay, and the gating is a regime switch. Lightning adds delays on dry fields.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(delay) with roof-type interaction and lightning indicator; compare calibration by roof type.

interactions.hypothesis: Extras equal tie after top 9 times failure to walk off; the failure probability depends on closer quality, so for elite closers the extras probability is lower for the same tie probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose extras frequency into tie and non-walk-off components and test closer effect.

interactions.hypothesis: KXMLBDELAY's text counts in-game weather stoppages as well as a delayed start, so extra innings add weather exposure only while no start delay has been recorded; once any start delay occurs the market is already Yes and game length no longer matters. The dependence on extras is therefore conditional on the pre-game weather state.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition delay frequency on extras flag in historical data and compare with start-only delay frequency.

interactions.hypothesis: Recorded delays follow a threshold in precipitation intensity and duration; light drizzle is played through while heavy rain triggers a tarp, so the response of delay probability to rain probability is steeply nonlinear above a threshold.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit logistic of recorded delay on forecast precipitation intensity and duration; test breakpoint.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold/saturating: delay probability low below about 30% precipitation chance, steep between 40-70%, saturating near 90%
nonlinearities.why: Delay requires rain or lightning to actually occur during play and be heavy enough, so the response to forecast probability is S-shaped.

nonlinearities.shape: Tie mass peaks at low totals: P(tie) falls convexly as expected total rises
nonlinearities.why: The diagonal of the joint distribution thins as variance grows, so tie probability is decreasing and convex in expected total.

nonlinearities.shape: Binary gate: closed roof reduces delay probability to near zero regardless of forecast
nonlinearities.why: The roof removes exposure, so weather inputs matter only when open.

nonlinearities.shape: Approximate threshold (assumed convention): a strike within about 8 miles commonly triggers a roughly 30-minute hold, independent of strike count
nonlinearities.why: League safety protocol makes delay a step function of lightning proximity rather than intensity. This is an assumed convention, not a published uniform MLB rule; the threshold distance and hold length vary by stadium and umpire crew.

mechanism_review.summary: Two event families share the archetype and are mechanically unrelated. Extra innings occur when the two teams' nine-inning run totals are equal, so the probability is the tie mass of the difference of two overdispersed run counts, adjusted by the structure that the home team skips the bottom ninth when ahead; it is highest in low-scoring, evenly matched games and is a few percentage points higher than naive Poisson-based estimates because runs correlate positively across teams through park and weather. Delay markets are weather-timing problems: a delay requires precipitation, lightning within the league's safety radius, or severe wind/temperature conditions overlapping the game window while the roof is open or absent, and the umpire crew and team officials decide to stop or hold play. The probability depends on forecast timing and convective structure rather than team quality, and on how the contract defines delay (start versus in-game, any duration). Both are low-to-moderate probability events where the contract's exact wording and the quality of timing information decide edge.

stages.name: Regulation score distribution and tie mass
stages.description: Extras occur only if the score is level after nine complete innings. The tie mass is the sum over k of P(away = k) P(home = k) with a positive dependence between teams, so a low expected total and a close pairing raise it. The home team's skipped bottom of the ninth does not create extras; it removes them in games where the home team leads.
stages.distribution: Tie probability about 8-10% of games; sensitive to total: low-total games tie more; positive team-run correlation raises tie mass.

stages.name: Late-inning resolution before extras
stages.description: Extras happen when the score is level after nine complete innings. The main routes are a tie after the top of the 9th that the home team fails to break, and a one-or-more-run visitor lead that the home team equalises without taking the lead; a home lead after 8.5 innings removes the bottom half entirely. The bottom-9 half-inning is a stopping-rule process: it ends the moment the home team takes the lead, so run totals are truncated and the P(level) depends on the closer, the due-up hitters and the deficit entering the half.
stages.distribution: Conditional probability of the home team scoring at least once in a tied bottom 9 is roughly 27-32% for a typical reliever (league P(run) per half-inning is about 0.27); lower against elite closers. The extras event is Bernoulli with a mixture over the entering run differential.

stages.name: Weather exposure over the game window
stages.description: Delay requires weather in the window: precipitation timing relative to first pitch and the expected 3-hour game, lightning within eight miles (league and stadium safety rules), heavy wind or cold in some venues, and a roof that is open, closed, or retractable with a decision made before first pitch. The same forecast yields different delay probabilities across parks with and without roofs and with different drainage.
stages.distribution: Binary event with probability about 5-10% overall, near 0 in domes and up to 30-50% on convectively active evenings.

stages.name: Decision and recording process
stages.description: Whether weather becomes an official delay depends on umpire and home-team judgement and on the way the delay is recorded: a start delayed by tarp, an in-game stoppage, a rain-shortened or suspended game, or a postponement. Short delays may not be recorded in the structured data, and a postponed game is not a delayed one under the sampled wording.
stages.distribution: Threshold decision with human judgement; recording rules produce a minimum recorded duration in data.

stages.name: Interaction between the two events
stages.description: Extras lengthen the game and thereby increase exposure to in-game weather delays, so a delay contract that counts in-game stoppages is mildly positively related to extras; start-delay contracts are unaffected. For the extras contract, a suspended game (weather) tied in the middle is not extras.
stages.distribution: Small positive dependence through game length; negligible for start delays.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Two live series with sampled rules, now filed here. KXMLBEXTRAS: Yes 'If at least 1 extra inning is played' in the named game, i.e. the score is level after nine complete innings (no secondary rules text). KXMLBDELAY: Yes if the game originally scheduled for the date 'is officially delayed due to weather', which 'includes a delayed start time as well as any suspension or stoppage of play after the event has begun due to weather'; delays caused solely by other reasons resolve No. Neither text addresses a game postponed before first pitch, a suspended game resumed later, or names a data source.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official linescore (innings played) for extras; official game log/box-score delay record for weather delays (MLB Stats API, box score 'delay' line); presumed, since neither sampled text names a source.
variants_and_edge_cases: The two contract families are unrelated mechanically: extras is a function of the run distribution (a regulation tie), delay is a weather-timing event unrelated to team quality, and a shared model would conflate them.

Delay definition counts both a delayed start time and any in-game weather stoppage regardless of duration, so even short (five-minute) stoppages count if recorded as official delays; a postponed game (no first pitch that day) is not described.

Extras requires the game to remain tied after the top and bottom of the ninth (the bottom is played only if the home team does not lead); a game called by weather while tied before the ninth is a suspension or shortened game, not extras.
A suspended game completed later with extra innings is attached to 'originally scheduled' date in the sampled wording but handling is unstated.

season_futures.label: Division winner, season wins, postseason futures and series
season_futures.target: Team season outcomes: division title, win total thresholds, playoff/pennant/title futures, postseason series winners, records and specials.
season_futures.mechanism: Futures integrate talent estimates (projection priors updated with run differential, not record) through the remaining schedule with uncertainty, then apply tiebreakers and bracket rules; postseason series switch to a game-level dynamic program using announced starters, rest, bullpen usage and home-field pattern. Long-horizon prices depend on rating uncertainty and slow information (injuries, trades); short-horizon series prices depend on pitching availability and shortened managerial hooks. Luck regression and tiebreaker formalities matter most in close races.

inputs.why: Monte Carlo of the remaining schedule and bracket.
Talent prior from projection systems.
Regress record luck to run differential.
Remaining schedule quality: future opponent quality, home/away split and days off shape expected wins for the remainder of the season.
Injuries to key players and depth.
Rotation quality, especially in October.
Bullpen quality for close games.
Seeding and tiebreaker rules: seeding, wild-card format and tiebreaker rules decide who plays whom and with what home field, determining futures settle paths.
Series state, rest and rotation for series markets.
Postseason pitching usage patterns.
League baselines for season specials.
Trades and call-ups: transactions and news change who plays and the team's strength with a lag before statistics catch up.
Futures benchmark: sharp sportsbook and exchange lines are a competing aggregation of information and the standard benchmark for fair probability.
Division, wildcard and win-total markets are tails of a schedule simulation with injury and rating uncertainty.
Provides the tail-width parameter the season simulation needs.
Seed and qualifier markets settle on seed and bracket, so ignoring tiebreakers misprices close races.
Matches the information relevant to series and title futures instead of full-season ratings.
A direct input to the remaining-schedule simulation that is not captured by season-to-date records.
Supplies the primary state of the win-total ladders that pythag_luck alone did not define.
Specifies the missing inputs for the matchup and games-hosted series.
Gives series MVP series a defined model instead of a market-price input.
Defines exposure for the playoff leader series, which previously had no inputs.
Gives KXMLBWORLD a national-team strength input; no club-level input in this archetype measures it.

interactions.hypothesis: Talent uncertainty x series length: greater uncertainty about true strength widens futures outcomes and short series compress the talent gap, so rating uncertainty and format interact.
Luck regression x tiebreakers: simulation should use expected wins for strength but formal tiebreakers for the ties, so regress luck first, apply rules second.
Injury state x remaining schedule: a long-term injury reduces strength for the remainder, with a larger effect when remaining opponents are strong or the margin for playoffs is thin.

The weight on run-based evidence versus the preseason prior is games/(games + k), so early in the season the prior dominates and late the record dominates; the posterior variance falls accordingly. The interaction between games played and each source determines tail width, so the two sources cannot be added with fixed weights.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit the weighting k by backtesting predicted rest-of-season win% at different dates; compare to fixed-weight blend.

interactions.hypothesis: A seller's loss of rest-of-season WAR matters most for teams still in the race, and its effect on win total is proportional to games remaining; opponent strength of those remaining games conditions the impact on wins, so the shift must enter the simulation, not the record.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate remaining games with and without shifts and measure change in P(win threshold).

interactions.hypothesis: Championship probability is convex in seed through the bye and bracket: a top-two division winner skips a round (one fewer series to win) and faces weaker opponents; the value of one extra win near the seeding boundary is large, so final-week wins have convex impact on title odds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute title probability by seed with a bracket simulation and compare marginal value of a win near boundaries.

interactions.hypothesis: In the postseason the rotation shortens, so the weight on top starters rises and day-by-day starter identity matters; the pitching regime changes at the start of the playoffs, so regular-season starter weights misprice series.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate series win probability with playoff weights versus season weights on historical series.

interactions.hypothesis: Uncertainty about team strength is shared across games and rounds, so series outcomes are positively correlated across a team's path: a team that is stronger than believed wins several series, which fattens the tails of championship probability relative to independent rounds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare title probability from simulations with shared strength draws versus independent per-series draws.

interactions.hypothesis: The chance of a long streak rises much faster than linearly in per-game win probability (P of an L-game run scales like p^L), so the strongest teams dominate the streak market more than their win-total edge suggests, and a team with an active streak near the league maximum late in the season is priced mostly off its next few games; games remaining cap the opportunity.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare simulated and realised league-maximum streaks by team quality decile over past seasons and check calibration of P(longest) for teams with active streaks.

interactions.hypothesis: For 2027 futures the model is a mixture over labour regimes: no stoppage (a normal 162-game season), a shortened season (fewer games, so more variance in standings and more upsets of strong teams) and a cancelled postseason (settlement unknown). Strong favourites lose value under shortened seasons because season-long talent edges matter less, so the regime weights interact with team strength rather than scaling all teams equally.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare championship probabilities of top-, middle- and bottom-tier teams under 60-, 120- and 162-game simulated seasons, using 2020 as a reference for a shortened season.

interactions.hypothesis: Best-record, worst-record and 100-loss outcomes are linked: teams share opponents, so one team's extra wins are another's losses, and the worst-record race is usually decided among two or three teams whose posteriors overlap. Ties at the extreme pay $1/N, so the joint probability of equal winning percentages near the end of the season changes expected payouts even when the leader is clear.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate the full league season jointly versus independently per team and compare predicted extreme and tie probabilities against settled seasons since 2000.

nonlinearities.shape: Variance falls hyperbolically with games played, with jumps at roster shocks
nonlinearities.why: Posterior precision adds linearly with games, so sd falls like 1/sqrt(n) and not linearly; shocks reset part of the uncertainty.

nonlinearities.shape: Logistic in log run ratio, which is close to linear in run differential over normal team ranges (exponent about 1.83); the relevant nonlinearity is the games-played shrinkage weight n/(n+k) on run-based evidence
nonlinearities.why: The claim of concavity at large run ratios is irrelevant for full-season totals; what matters is how fast pythagenpat evidence outweighs the preseason prior, which is the weight n/(n+156) specified in the talent-posterior input.

nonlinearities.shape: Compressing S-shape: series win probability is a steep logistic of per-game edge, with best-of-7 amplification
nonlinearities.why: Longer series amplify edges, but the amplification is limited, so title futures compress toward 50% pairs.

nonlinearities.shape: Cliff at the seeding boundary
nonlinearities.why: One extra win can change a bye, opponent and home field, giving a step in title probability at the boundary.

nonlinearities.shape: order-statistic concentration
nonlinearities.why: The probability of holding the best or worst record rises steeply with a team's mean relative to its nearest rival, so small posterior shifts late in the season move the extreme markets far more than win-total ladders.

mechanism_review.summary: Futures integrate three layers. First, a team's true talent is uncertain: a preseason projection prior is updated by run differential (not record) with a posterior standard deviation that shrinks through the season and jumps with roster changes and injuries. Second, the remaining schedule converts talent into a distribution of wins, with binomial game noise of about six wins over a full season on top of talent uncertainty, which gives the wide win-total distributions the ladders price. Third, standings are turned into postseason fates by rules: division winners, wild cards, byes for the top division winners, tiebreakers decided by head-to-head and divisional records, and a bracket in which each series is a dynamic program over announced starters, rest, bullpen leverage and home-field pattern. Short series compress the talent gap, so championship probabilities for even good teams are low and depend on rotation depth and bullpen top-end in October, not on regular-season records. Season extremes (best and worst record, 100 losses, longest winning and losing streaks) are order statistics or run lengths over thirty teams' game sequences, with $1/N tie splits and no tiebreakers; matchup, seed and division-of-champion markets are bracket-path events or unions of team title events. The World Baseball Classic market is a national-team short tournament with its own rosters, pitch limits and single-elimination rounds. Award and leader series sit in season_leaders_and_awards.

stages.name: Talent posterior and uncertainty
stages.description: A team's strength is a distribution, not a number: a preseason projection built from player aging curves and depth charts is the prior, run differential adjusted for schedule and luck updates it, and roster changes (trades, injuries, call-ups) shift it. The posterior standard deviation determines how wide the win-total and title distributions are and decreases with games played.
stages.distribution: Normal-like posterior on true win percentage with sd falling from about 0.04 in April to about 0.028-0.03 by September (the data add precision slowly because a season of games identifies talent only to about 0.03); jumps at injuries and deadline trades.

stages.name: Remaining schedule to wins distribution
stages.description: Given talent, wins to date plus the sum of remaining game outcomes with per-game probability depending on opponent strength, park, rest and the unbalanced division schedule; binomial noise dominates close thresholds and is correlated with talent uncertainty, so the distribution is a mixture of binomials. For any 2027 future the number of games and whether a postseason is held are themselves uncertain under a labour-stoppage scenario, which shrinks win totals and, in the extreme, cancels the championship.
stages.distribution: Mixture of binomials; sd of final wins about 6.5 for 162 games from game noise plus 3-5 from talent uncertainty early.

stages.name: Standings, tiebreakers and seeding
stages.description: Division winners, three wild cards and byes are decided on final records; ties are broken by head-to-head record, divisional record and other criteria with no tiebreaker game, so the same win total can map to different outcomes. The seed assigned at the start of the postseason sets the bracket path and home-field, which matters for the seed and qualifier contracts.
stages.distribution: Discrete fate with probability concentrated at near-boundary records; tiebreaker outcomes are deterministic functions of records.

stages.name: Postseason series dynamic program
stages.description: Each series is a sequence of games with a rotation order, rest and travel days, shortened starter leashes and use of top relievers; teams' per-game win probabilities differ by announced starter and by the playoff-adjusted lineup and bullpen strength; game outcomes are correlated through unobserved strength. Championship probability is the product over rounds of series win probabilities with path dependence.
stages.distribution: Series win probability compresses talent gap (a 60% single-game team wins a best-of-7 about 71%); path-dependent mixture.

stages.name: Season extremes and bracket pairings
stages.description: Several series are not functions of one team's win total. Best and worst record and 100+ losses are tails of the joint distribution of thirty teams' records, correlated through shared schedules, with $1/N splits on tied winning percentage and no tiebreakers. The longest winning and losing streak markets are maximum run lengths over 162-game sequences for all teams, depending on per-game win probabilities, current streaks and the league maximum to date. Matchup markets resolve on which two teams qualify for a series through a fixed bracket, and division- or league-of-champion markets are unions over member teams' title paths.
stages.distribution: Record extremes: order statistics with mass concentrated on two to four teams and frequent ties at the extreme; streaks: extreme-value with a heavy upper tail (league maximum typically 9-12 games); matchup and union markets: categorical over bracket paths, moving in steps as series end.

stages.name: World Baseball Classic national-team tournament
stages.description: The World Baseball Classic winner depends on which major-league players each federation actually rosters (participation decisions, club and insurance restrictions on pitchers), how that talent maps into a few games under pitch-count limits that cap starters at short outings, pool play with run-based tiebreakers and then single-elimination knockout rounds where one game decides advancement. Depth of relief pitching matters more than in MLB because starters are limited, and the tournament is played in March before players are at full workload.
stages.distribution: Strongly favourite-compressed: single-elimination games at roughly 55-70% for the better side give even the strongest roster a title probability well below one half; pool-stage tiebreakers add discrete jumps.

talent_strength.note: Club prior, update and uncertainty; national-team roster strength for the World Baseball Classic.

distribution_variance.note: Mixture of binomials with shared strength uncertainty, order statistics of thirty teams' records, and extreme-value distributions of the longest winning and losing streaks.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Remaining schedule, tiebreakers and labour-stoppage season length for 2027 futures.

efficiency_conversion.note: There is no per-opportunity conversion rate at the futures level; team run-prevention and run-scoring efficiency enter through talent estimates (projections and pythag) rather than a separate conversion variable.

officiating_rules.note: Officials play no role in club season outcomes; the World Baseball Classic round pitch-count limits change how talent converts to wins and are encoded in the national-team strength measurement; the mercy rule is not modelled (sf_wbc_rules).

contract_review.settlement_definition: Fifty-five live series of season-long team outcomes after the reconciliation; all but KXMLBWS (title-only) have sampled rules. Team win-total ladders (KXMLBWINS-<TEAM>, all thirty teams) pay Yes if the team has at least N wins in the 2026 regular season ('Ties do not count as wins'); division winners pay on the 2026 division title; pennant (KXMLBAL, KXMLBNL), World Series and champion-division/league futures pay on the title, with division or league affiliation fixed 'when that championship begins'; qualifier markets (NLCSQUAL, ALCSQUAL, PLAYOFFS) pay if the team reaches that stage; KXMLBSEEDWIN pays if a team holding the named seed at the start of the postseason wins the championship; KXMLBMATCHUP resolves 'immediately upon qualification' of the named pairing; KXMLBWSOUTCOME pays on the exact winner and runner-up. Season extremes: best and worst record by winning percentage ($1/N rounded down to the cent on ties, no tiebreakers), longest winning and losing streaks ($1/N on shared streaks), and 100+ losses (no tie branch). KXMLBWORLD pays on the World Baseball Classic winner (2026 tournament). KXMLB includes a 2027 championship future that depends on a 2027 season being played after the CBA expires on Dec 1 2026. No text names a source or addresses a cancelled or shortened season.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official MLB standings and postseason results; World Baseball Classic official results for KXMLBWORLD; not named in the sampled rules.
variants_and_edge_cases: Same archetype mixes regular-season win ladders (binomial-like with talent uncertainty), division titles and playoff qualification (standings and tiebreakers), title futures (bracket dynamic program), seed and division/league unions, bracket pairings, season extremes (best/worst record, longest winning and losing streaks, 100 losses) and a national-team tournament; each needs a different generator.

Seed futures fix seed at the start of the postseason; tiebreakers (head-to-head, divisional record) decide seeds without a game-163 under the current format, so tiebreaker data are required for close races, while record-extreme markets explicitly ignore tiebreakers and split ties $1/N.
Postseason qualifiers resolve at the moment the series is reached; some markets (NLCSQUAL) are determined by winning the division series, so the probability is conditional on the bracket path.

KXMLBWS is the only series without sampled rules; no sampled text addresses a cancelled postseason or a shortened season, which matters for the 2027 championship future (KXMLB) given the CBA expiry on Dec 1 2026 (in 1994 the World Series was cancelled), and for any record, streak or 100-loss market whose season is shortened.

KXMLBWORLD (World Baseball Classic) is a separate competition with national rosters, pool play followed by single elimination, pitch-count limits and mercy rules (to my knowledge); its one-line text is silent on cancellation, tied pool standings and rain-shortened games.

KXMLBDIVWINNER (2025 sample) and KXMLBCHAMPDIVISION (2026) are the same object, the division of the champion; the 2025 text has no affiliation clause, the 2026 text fixes affiliation when the championship begins.

season_leaders_and_awards.label: Season leaders, player stat totals and awards
season_leaders_and_awards.target: Leader of a statistical category, a player's season total threshold, or winner of an award (MVP, Cy Young, ROY).
season_leaders_and_awards.mechanism: Season-stat and leader outcomes are current total plus rest-of-season rate times opportunity times availability, so a competitor-level simulation (with correlated team context, injury risk, and qualification rules for rate stats) gives probabilities. Awards add a voter model: production rank, team success and narrative under a specific ballot structure and timing, with finalists as information events. Early-season leaders mostly reflect luck, so regressing rates is the main lever, while late-season markets are dominated by games remaining and injuries.

True-talent rate for hitters: a hitter's quality per plate appearance (on-base skill, power, contact quality) determines hits, bases, runs and RBIs.
True-talent rate for pitchers.
Opportunity (PA/IP) projection.
Injury risk to contenders: absences change lineup/rotation composition and late scratches can void or reprice player markets.
Regress hot streaks in HR totals.
Electorate and ballot structure.
WAR and counting stats voters see.
Team success and storylines: voters respond to storylines and team success beyond raw metrics, creating systematic deviations from WAR rankings.
Team outcomes correlate with votes.
Stat source and settlement date.
The probability a player finishes first is the probability his final total exceeds every rival's; correlations and games remaining set it.
Provides the estimand the voter hypotheses refer to and distinguishes finalist from winner markets.
Defines the candidate set for the ROY market, a first-order determinant of probabilities.
The finalist rule gives a No branch tied to the announcement calendar, so its probability must be estimated.
Gives a specific input for the monthly and weekly awards filed in this archetype, otherwise unaddressed.
Triple Crown is rare, so the joint distribution is crucial.
Defines the selection process for the All-Star series that previously had no stage or input.
Gives the exhibition-game series a defined model.
Defines the lottery mechanism for the draft series.
Defines the joint structure for combination markets.

interactions.hypothesis: Rate x opportunity x availability: final total = current + rate x games remaining x P(play), so injury hazard and role changes interact with talent for leaders.
Qualification x rate stats: borderline players qualify only by PA accrual, so playing time and qualification rules interact in batting-average or ERA leader markets.
Production rank x team success x ballot timing: voters weigh WAR with team outcome and cast ballots at a specific time, so late-season changes matter only before the deadline.

Final total equals current plus rate times games remaining times the probability of playing, so injury hazard and role changes scale the projected increment; for a leader with a small lead and a high injury risk, availability dominates talent differences.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute leader probability with and without injury hazard multipliers; check calibration in late-season leader races.

interactions.hypothesis: Rate-stat leaders need the plate-appearance qualification (3.1 PA per scheduled team game for batters), so a borderline hitter's probability of leading a rate category depends on whether he accrues enough PAs; just below the threshold the official shortfall provision still lets him lead if hitless at-bats added up to the minimum leave his rate on top, so the threshold is soft for batters. No equivalent provision is known for the ERA title (1 inning per team game), which stays a hard cut (unverified; contract wording unseen).
interactions.how_to_test: Model qualification as a stopping rule on PA accrual and compare leader probabilities with and without it.

interactions.hypothesis: Voters trade off WAR and narrative and team success nonlinearly: beyond a certain WAR gap the narrative matters little, and below it a division title can flip the ranking; the interaction between production gap and team success is not additive.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate Plackett-Luce with interaction of WAR gap and team playoff flag and test improvement.

interactions.hypothesis: Finalist markets settle on a top-three rank only if finalists are announced before the winner. The rank event and the announcement-timing event are different processes; the interaction of interest is whether announcement timing depends on how tight the field is or on the award's calendar, not their product.
interactions.how_to_test: Test whether the announcement-before-winner indicator varies with field concentration or award type across 2015-2025, rather than assuming independence.

interactions.hypothesis: Triple Crown needs one player to lead three correlated stats; the joint probability depends on the covariance of HR and RBI (strongly positive) and AVG (weakly related), so the probability is much larger than an independent product for a power hitter with a big lead but small when AVG is contested. The stated covariances and the 1.5-sd collapse are illustrative and must be estimated.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate stat covariance from historical seasons; compare joint simulation to product of marginals in past races.

interactions.hypothesis: A series-MVP or playoff-leader probability is the product of team advancement (games played) and the player's share of production or credit given those games; the same hitter is a long shot if his team is likely to be swept and a favourite if a seven-game series is likely, so team and player components cannot be added.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit series-MVP outcomes 2000-2025 with P(team wins series) x credit share versus additive and share-only baselines and compare log loss.

interactions.hypothesis: A staff's strikeout lead depends on who pitches the remaining innings: a deadline acquisition of a high-strikeout starter or the loss of an ace to injury shifts the staff K% for the rest of the season, and the effect on the leader market is large only when the race is close, since a staff ahead by a hundred strikeouts in August is rarely caught.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare rest-of-season staff K% before and after deadline moves and test whether leader probabilities updated on roster changes beat a static staff projection.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in lead size: probability of finishing first rises steeply when the lead exceeds one standard deviation of remaining production
nonlinearities.why: Leader probability is a tail event of the difference of two noisy totals; it saturates near one when the lead exceeds the plausible remaining production.

nonlinearities.shape: Qualification threshold at 3.1 PA per scheduled team game with a shortfall exception: a batter just below it can still win a rate title if his rate stays highest after hitless at-bats are added to reach the minimum (official scoring rule, wording for this contract unverified)
nonlinearities.why: The probability is not zero below the threshold: a borderline player with a large rate lead remains a contender, so the PA-shortfall must be modelled rather than a hard cut; the record's hard-zero treatment mis-specifies such candidates.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating: marginal vote probability per WAR falls as WAR gap grows
nonlinearities.why: Voters recognise a clear best player; further WAR advantage adds little, but near parity small differences matter.

nonlinearities.shape: Strong shrinkage of early-season totals toward projection, flattening later
nonlinearities.why: Early-season award leaders should be shrunk heavily toward projection because counting production stabilises slowly, and the weight on observed totals rises nonlinearly with games played.

mechanism_review.summary: Awards and leaders are of two types. Statistical outcomes (season leaders, Triple Crown, season thresholds) equal current totals plus rest-of-season rate times opportunities times availability, so the probability that a player finishes first is the probability his final total exceeds every rival's, with correlations through teams and parks and with rate-stat qualification rules deciding who is eligible. Voted outcomes (MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, finalists, Gold Glove, Silver Slugger, All-Star) are produced by a ballot of a specific electorate that ranks candidates on a mixture of production (WAR variants, counting stats), team success and narrative, with ballots cast at a fixed date and finalists announced before winners. The finalist market is a rank-three event, which is easier to predict than the winner, with a timing condition. A first-principles model uses a production model for statistical races and a rank-ordered voter model (Plackett-Luce) for awards, with candidate sets restricted by eligibility. Early-season leaders are mostly luck so regression of rates is critical; late-season markets are dominated by remaining games and injuries. After the reconciliation the archetype also holds postseason MVP and playoff-leader markets (team advancement times player credit), Manager and Executive of the Year (team surprise versus projection), and single-hitter season counting thresholds (50 HR, 50 HR plus 40 SB). The team-strikeout leader market (KXMLBTEAMSTAT) is a thirty-team order statistic of batters faced times staff strikeout rate.

stages.name: Candidate set and eligibility
stages.description: Each market has a candidate set determined by rules: rookie status for ROY, qualifying PA/IP for rate leaders, league membership, position for Gold Glove and Silver Slugger, and active roster for All-Star. The set is smaller than the full player pool, and eligibility changes (call-ups, injuries) change the field.
stages.distribution: Small candidate set (3-10 realistic contenders) with long tail of near-zero probabilities.

stages.name: Production to date and rest-of-season projection
stages.description: For statistical races final total = current total + rest-of-season rate x games remaining x probability of playing; rate is the true-talent estimate regressed from observed performance (HR/FB, BABIP), and opportunity depends on lineup slot, platoon and team schedule. Correlation across contenders arises from shared opponents and parks.
stages.distribution: Sum of a fixed current total and a compound future; right-skewed for HR, near-normal for rate stats with qualifiers.

stages.name: Voter model for awards
stages.description: Ballots rank candidates; each voter's ranking combines production metrics (WAR variants, counting stats), team success (playoff berth, division title) and narrative (milestones, comeback), with systematic biases (pitchers vs hitters in MVP, closers in Cy Young). Point systems aggregate ranks to a winner and finalists. The outcome is a rank distribution, not a single winner. The electorate differs by award (writers, retired relievers, fans/players, executives), so the rank-model coefficients are fitted per electorate and pooled only within the BBWAA awards.
stages.distribution: Rank distribution over few candidates; multinomial-logit or Plackett-Luce with correlated voter noise.

stages.name: Announcement timing and information events
stages.description: Finalists are announced about a week or two before winners, and ballots are cast before the postseason; markets that settle on announcements depend on whether and when these events occur. Finalist announcements are strong information events for winner markets.
stages.distribution: Discrete timing events with known calendar; announcement conditions create No branches.

stages.name: Period and joint-leader variants
stages.description: Monthly and weekly awards select players over short windows from committee judgement of production in that window, while Triple Crown requires leading three correlated categories (batting average, HR, RBI) simultaneously, with rate-stat qualification; these are distinct joint models.
stages.distribution: Short-window noisy production (monthly) and joint order statistic (Triple Crown); rare event.

stages.name: All-Star selection, postseason MVP and award combinations
stages.description: All-Star selection combines fan-vote phases, a player vote and commissioner or roster-fill rules. Series MVPs are chosen almost always from the winning team, so a player's chance is his team's series-win probability times his share of the credit (a few big games, a starter's two wins). The playoff runs leader is a race whose exposure is the number of playoff games each team plays, and award combinations need the joint distribution of correlated award outcomes.
stages.distribution: Selection: Bernoulli over vote tallies with a discrete roster-fill step; series MVP: product of a series-win probability and a concentrated credit share; playoff leader: order statistic over very unequal exposure; combinations: positively correlated joint outcomes.

stages.name: Manager awards and season counting thresholds
stages.description: Manager of the Year votes reward wins over preseason expectation, a division title or a turnaround, with ballots cast before the postseason, so the input is the team's surprise relative to projection rather than its record. The 50 home run and 50 HR plus 40 SB markets are threshold events of one hitter's regular-season counts, driven by current totals, remaining plate appearances and the correlation of power and speed through playing time.
stages.distribution: Manager award: concentrated rank distribution over two or three surprise teams; counting thresholds: rare joint tail that collapses once the pace falls behind.

stages.name: Team pitching-staff strikeout leader
stages.description: The team leading in strikeouts thrown is the maximum over thirty staffs of strikeouts to date plus remaining batters faced times the staff's strikeout rate, where the rate is a weighted mix of rotation and bullpen pitchers' projected K% and changes with injuries and deadline trades; extra-inning games and doubleheaders add batters faced. Ties at the top pay $1/N, which matters only when two staffs are within a few strikeouts in the final week.
stages.distribution: Order statistic of near-normal staff totals (season sd roughly 40-60 strikeouts from rate uncertainty and volume); probability concentrated on two or three high-strikeout staffs, with tie mass negligible except at the very end.

talent_strength.note: True-talent rates, production metrics and team surprise for manager awards.

game_context_script.note: Team success enters votes through award_narrative; series-MVP credit is conditional on the team winning the series.

pace_volume.note: Regular-season PA/IP opportunity and playoff games-played exposure.

efficiency_conversion.note: The only conversion input, HR/FB regression, was audited WEAK and subsumed by rate projection; leader and award markets use the projected rate directly, so no separate conversion input is claimed.

distribution_variance.note: Order statistics, rank distributions and joint threshold tails.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Narrative, ballot timing, games remaining.

settlement_contract.note: Source agencies, announcement conditions, tie handling.

opponent_matchup.note: Season leaders and awards are accumulated over hundreds of games against the whole league, so single-game matchup effects average out; the only matchup-like factor is remaining schedule strength, which is a minor term in the rest-of-season rate.

coaching_scheme.note: Manager decisions affect leaders through lineup slot and playing time (included in expected PA) and for Gold Glove/Silver Slugger the voters are managers, covered in the voter model; no separate scheme factor drives the outcome.

environment.note: Park and weather enter the rest-of-season rate through projections and are not separate drivers at this horizon; home-park effects on counting stats are in the player's projected rate.

officiating_rules.note: Official scoring changes can alter totals slightly and tie handling matters for leaders, but these are covered in settlement; umpire effects are negligible at season scale.
